Fish assemblages in floodplain lakes in a Neotropical river during the wet season (Magdalena River, Colombia) Carlos Granado-Lorencio*,†, Alejandra Gulfo†, Frank Alvarez†, Luz Fernanda Jiménez-Segura†, Juan David Carvajal-Quintero† and Andrés Hernández-Serna† * Department of Plant Biology and Ecology, Faculty of Biology, University of Sevilla, Box 1095, 41080 Sevilla, Spain † Ichthyology Group, Sciences Institute, University of Antioquia, Medellín, Colombia (Accepted 20 February 2012) Abstract: A number of studies have pointed out that abiotic factors and recolonization dynamics appear to be more important than biotic interactions in structuring river–fish assemblages. In this paper, we studied the fish assemblages in 27 floodplain lakes, with perennial connection to the river, in the middle section of the Magdalena River (Colombia), to examine spatial pattern in freshwater fish diversity in relation to some environmental parameters. Our objective was to examine relationships between floodplain-lake fish communities and environmental variables associated with lake morphology, water chemistry and river–floodplain connectivity in a large river–floodplain ecosystem. During the study, a total of 18 237 fish were caught from 50 species (regional richness; 17 were migrants and 33 residents). In the present study, the most diverse order was Characiformes with 20 species, followed by Siluriformes, with 19 species. Characidae and Loricariidae were the richest families. The range of species richness (local richness) varied between five and 39 species. Similarity of local assemblages (using the presence–absence data) depends on the distance between lakes. A positive relationship was observed between the Ln of the total abundance of each species and the number of lakes where they were found. Out of all the environmental parameters taken in the lakes, only the size (Log Area) and relative perimeter length are significantly related to local assemblage species richness. It has not been possible to demonstrate that the connectivity (distance) from lakes to the main river can be considered a predictor of the local richness. Key Words: distance decay, fish, floodplain lakes, local richness, river INTRODUCTION Patterns of species co-occurrence have been widely investigated by ecologists (Jackson et al. 1992, Peres-Neto 2004). Fish communities are structured by effects working at a regional scale, where abiotic factors limit the species distributions; and at a local scale, where biotic factors determine species survival within a system (Gaston 2000, Thompson 2009). However, in highly variable aquatic systems, abiotic factors appear to be more important with little or no influence of biotic factors (Fisher & Lindenmayer 2002, Granado-Lorencio et al. 2007, Snodgrass et al. 1995, Suárez et al. 2004, Taylor & Warren 2001). In large tropical rivers, rainfall-driven hydrology is a key factor in the seasonality of aquatic environments (Sanderson et al. 2005). The flood-pulse concept (FPC) identifies seasonal hydrology as the major force structuring stream–fish assemblages (Araújo et al. 2009, Junk et al. 1989). During the flood pulse, the majority of water bodies become interconnected (floodplains) and the fish are free to disperse throughout the floodplain (Godoy et al. 1999). Floodplain lakes connected with the river by channels are open systems (Saint-Paul et al. 2000), and are typical ecotopes of large lowland rivers (Schomaker & Wolter 2011). In Neotropical floodplains, the flood cycle (pulse) associated with alteration of dry and rainy seasons produces major changes in fish communities (Rodríguez & Lewis 1994), and it acts as an intermediate disturbance. Because of high environmental variability, species assemblage organization has been portrayed as highly stochastic, without any apparent overall organizational pattern (Lowe-McConnell 1987, Lowe et al. 2006). However, more recent studies have seemingly found non-random associations of fishes within the floodplain (Petry et al. 2003, Winemiller 1996). Studies on the structure and dynamics of fish assemblages of permanent water bodies in different floodplain river systems indicate that these assemblages are structured by a combination of environmental variables, as well as by the pool of species available during the period in which the water bodies are permanently connected to the river (Fernandes et al. 2010). Certain environmental variables (hypoxia, depth, transparency, local-scale habitat, size and drainage area) have been considered to be good predictors of the richness of local associations of fish, within the floodplain (Montaña & Winemiller 2010). A study of the factors that control species richness in floodplain lakes requires information about the taxonomy and distribution of the species. Information is more extensive on fish species from temperate rivers and big tropical rivers than on fish species of floodplain lakes. Therefore, the first aim of this study was to catalogue fish species (ichthyofauna survey) and examine the fish richness in tropical floodplain lakes, during the high-water season. For this study, we selected 27 lakes from the Magdalena river, which vary in morphological and limnological characteristics. The fish caught were identified taxonomically and the sampling data were used to calculate the total abundance. The second aim was to determine the main factors that control local species richness (lake community). We test the following hypotheses: (1) there is an relationship between abundance and regional occupancy (%) in fish species of the floodplain lakes, (2) the area is related to the species richness of the lake (species–area relationship, SAR), (3) the distance to the main river (connectivity) is a predictive variable of local richness, and (4) the geographical distance between lakes has a relationship to the similarity in fish assemblages found in them (community similarity decay). METHODS The Magdalena River is 1612 km long and drains a 257 438-km² basin. The principal tributaries are the Cauca, Sogamoso, San Jorge and César Rivers. The average precipitation for the valley measured in run-off is 2050 mm y⁻¹. The lowest values are recorded for the December–January and July–August periods, and the highest between April–May and October–November (twice-yearly peak flooding). The annual mean discharge (data for 1975–1995) from the Magdalena River in the locality of Calamar (112 km upstream of the estuary) is 7200 m³ s⁻¹ (Restrepo & Jerfve 2000). The physical structure of the system comprises a meandering river channel with numerous connected and isolated lakes (lakes vary in size and degree of connection). The main types of habitats in floodplain lakes are herbaceous vegetation (aquatic macrophytes) and open water. The relative proportion of the habitats varies both regionally and seasonally. The whole middle and lower Magdalena River is not fragmented by dams and is still characterized by highly variable hydrological conditions. While some floodplain lakes become permanently cut off from the main flow of the river and remain closed (isolated), others remain open with perennial connection with the river. Twenty-seven connected lakes were studied, all in the midsection of the Magdalena River basin, between the localities of Puerto Boyacá and Barrancabermeja (840.92 km; Figure 1). The study area is centred at 6°04′N–7°26′N, 73°57′W–74°31′W (GPS derived). The selection was based on lake surface area and permanent connectivity with the main river. These lakes were selected to represent a range of size (4–2300 ha) and degree of human impact (Table 1). Lakes were sampled during the wet season, because of its near-maximum species richness and stability in water level. Ten lakes were sampled at the beginning of November 2008 (Palagua, Samaria, El Encanto, Rio Viejo, Barbacoas, Chucurí, El Opón, Juan Esteban, Tabacurú, Bija) and the remaining 17 in 2010, at the same month, coinciding with the second peak flooding. The sampling method was the same for all the lakes. Water parameters were measured for 24 h every 4 h. At each fishing site, dissolved oxygen concentration (DO in mg L⁻¹), water temperature (T in °C) and conductivity (μS) were measured in situ. DO (dissolved oxygen) and temperature were measured in the water column every metre. The maximum depth (m) of lakes was determined by sonar. For each lake, the area and perimeter length were calculated for the period of high water level. An index used to quantify this is called the shoreline development (DI). This index compares the minimum possible circumference of the lake, given a specific surface area (i.e. a perfect circle), to the actual circumference of the lake and its surface area. A value of 1 for shoreline development is a perfect circle and a larger value means that the shoreline is highly dissected. Lakes with high shoreline development are often naturally productive relative to those with low shoreline development. The shortest distance between lakes and the river were measured on maps (1: 100 000) from Google Earth. We use the length of the channel (measured in the field) that links the lake to the main river as a measure of connectivity; Tockner et al. (1999) consider that this distance is a good predictor for this structural variable. Prior to statistical analyses, all variables except pH and temperature were logarithmically transformed in order to approximate normal distributions. The measurements for environmental variables were analysed using a one-way ANOVA with the aim of discovering differences between periods, as well as between habitats for each period (Bonferroni correction included). In order to estimate the total species richness, sampling was designed for each of the various existing habitats. In all the lakes, one sampling station was chosen within each of these four macrohabitats: littoral with trees, littoral without trees, open water, and the connecting channel between the lake and main river. All were sampled simultaneously. Because sampling effort was constant across samples, it was not necessary to adjust richness estimates using rarefaction or other techniques to account for different sampling techniques or sample sizes. The fish were collected using experimental multifilament gillnets, formed from panels measuring 100 × 3 m, in nine different sizes (from 2 to 10 cm stretched mesh). This kind of technique for capture has been used in the studies of associations of fish in oxbow lakes (Winemiller et al. 2000). The nets were set out for 24 h, and checked every 4 h, with the intention of avoiding phenomena such as predators and decomposition due to the high temperature of the water. Fishes were classified as sedentary or short-distance migrant species based on available regional information. Catch per site was standardized according to the length of bank fished and the catch per unit effort (CPUE) determined as fish caught per 100 m. The standardized fish densities were used to calculate basic fish-assemblage metrics, like relative abundance (%) of species and richness. In all analyses for a lake, only the abundances and richness of taxa present at that lake were used. We used the Spearman’s rank correlation coefficient to test the occupancy-abundance relationship. We define the richness of species in a lake as local richness (LR, \( \alpha \)-diversity), and the analysis of all the lakes taken together as regional richness (RR, \( \gamma \)-diversity). We analysed the similarities of assemblages using only presence–absence data. Previous studies have shown that taxonomic patterns may differ when using the presence–absence or abundance data (La Sorte & McKinney 2007). In order to analyse whether the geographical distance between lakes has any relationship to the similarity in associations of fishes found in them (community similarity decay; Nekola & White 1999), the Sørensen index was applied (\( S = C/\alpha \); where C represents common species and \( \alpha \) the average richness for the two lakes), and the Figure 2. Scatterplot of abundance (Ln) versus regional occupancy (%) of the fish species collected. Names in bold represent migratory fish species. The figure was divided in relation to the mean values for each variable for the total number of species and lakes. Fish species are represented using the codes from Appendix 1. geographical distances between lakes were also calculated (using Google Map). Distance decay often is examined using linear geographic distance (Maloney & Munguía 2011). Distance decay is used to describe the decay in ecological similarity of assemblages between two sites as a function of their distance apart along an environmental gradient. Regression distance-decay models are fitted by calculating the ecological similarity between each pair of sites on a scatterplot of similarity vs. distance (x-axis). As the pairwise similarity values and distances are not truly independent in a statistical sense (each fish community is used in more than one pairwise comparison), we use average similarity and average distance for each lake. The significance of each regression model was tested using a randomization approach. The general model was conducted using software package Statistica 6.0. The study of species–area relationships (SARs) has a long tradition in ecology and the construction of SARs is one of the most frequently used methods to estimate species number at different spatial scales (Lomolino 2000). In this study, the data were fitted to the power model (ln (S) = z ln (A) + c). RESULTS A total of 18 237 individuals were recorded representing 50 species (regional richness). Characiformes (38%) and Siluriformes (36%) were the best represented orders. We observed 50 fish species (Appendix 1). The most frequent species in all catches were Cyphocharax magdalenae (29.3%) and Roeboides dayi (20.3%), followed by Caquetaia kraussii (14.6%) and Trachelyopterus insignis (12.8%), all of them with a sedentary life style. The range of richness of species (local richness) varied between 9 and 39 species. In Figure 2, the species caught were ordered on the basis of their overall Ln regional abundance and geographical range (% of lakes occupied). We observed 50 species, of which 22 were dominant, two were accidental, three common and 23 were rare (in relation to the mean values of the total number of species and lakes, 3.87% and 42.3%, respectively). The species found in all the lakes studied (100% incidence) were sedentary species: Caquetaia kraussii and Cyphocharax magdalenae. At the local scale, the relationship between migratory and sedentary species was significant and positive in all the lakes in terms of local richness (r = 0.79, P = 0.0009). A significant relationship was observed between the total abundance of each species (ln-transformed) and the number of lakes where they were found (n = 50, r_s = 0.93, P = 0.000001). Out of all the measurements taken in the lakes, only lake size (log(Area) was significantly correlated to the local richness of species (n = 27, r = 0.69, P = 0.0009) (Figure 3). We found that lake shoreline development had significant effect on species richness (n = 27, r = 0.48, P = 0.0068). The other environmental variables (including connectivity) were not significant in any of the multiple regressions; many habitat characteristics were significantly correlated. Similarity in fish communities decreased with distance. A linear regression provided a good fit to these data (averaged for each lake). Our results show that the Figure 3. DISCUSSION The Neotropical region harbours the world’s richest freshwater ichthyofauna, with more than 2500 species (Böhlke et al. 1978). The ichthyofauna of South American rivers is dominated by ostariophysan fishes (Characiformes over Siluriformes and Gymnotiformes). The families Anostomidae, Chilodontidae, Curimatidae and Prochilodontidae inhabit most river systems throughout tropical and subtropical South America and southern Central America (Albert & Reis 2011, Carolsfield et al. 2004). In the present study, the most diverse order was Characiformes with seven families and 20 species, followed by Siluriformes, six families and 19 species. Characidae and Loricariidae were the most diverse (seven genera). It is interesting to observe that there is a maximum of three species within each genus, and that most genera are represented by only one species. Lowe-McConnell (1987) explained high dominance of small characiformes in tropical fish communities mainly by the capacity of these species to use oxygen in the upper portion of the water column. Two variables were consistently related to the species richness: area and shoreline development. Other variables such as depth, DO, conductivity, temperature and distance to the main river were not significant in any of the multiple regressions. The lack of relationship between these variables and the fish richness in floodplain lakes could be accounted for by sampling limitations (type II error) or could represent a real lack of effect. Since we studied 27 lakes, the statistical resolution was reasonable despite the variability in catch. A more probable hypothesis is that these variables had a weak effect, if any, on species richness. Lake depth is often an important variable to explain fish richness and fish abundance. Winemiller et al. (2000) found a direct relationship between these variables in oxbow lakes of the Brazos River, USA. Suárez et al. (2004) and Tejerina-Garro et al. (1998) reported depth as one of the main environmental structuring factors of fish communities of the Pantanal and Araguaia River. Lake depth had a weak effect on the species richness of lakes in our study. Even if the connectivity (distance) to the main channel can be considered a predictive variable, indicating the richness of a lake, or at least in relation to migratory species as has been demonstrated in certain Amazon floodplain lakes (Granado-Lorencio et al. 2005), in our study it has not been possible to demonstrate this. In the lakes studied by Bertolo & Magnan (2006) connectivity had little effect on fish species richness; and Tejerina-Garro et al. (1998) verified that connectivity had no apparent effect on community structure. This may be because of the varying hydrological behaviour of the river, or the different capacities of diverse species to colonize or simply that the range of lengths of the connecting channels was not sufficient. Comparisons of tropical fish community structure in lake surveys conducted at regional or supra-regional scales have detected predictable links between community structure and environmental variation (Tejerina-Garro et al. 1998). Principally, the structure of fish assemblages can be produced by two different processes: species-specific colonization and/or dispersal potential and species-specific vulnerability to extinction. If it was generated through colonization, then species colonize sites located at different distances from the common source (main river). Species with greater capacity for dispersal are able to cover longer distances, and colonize more distant sites, than those which are either less mobile or sedentary. The similarity between species at sites demonstrates a more or less strong negative relationship to the geographical distance between them. This pattern has been observed in freshwater ecosystems (Taylor & Warren 2001). McAbendroth et al. (2005) indicate that the species with more limited capacity for dispersal occupy fewer sites than the migrant species. In our study, the two most abundant species (Caquetaia kraussi and Cyphocharax magdalenae) are present in the 27 lakes in the study; they are floodplain specialists but are not migratory species (both have sedentary behaviour; Galvis & Mójica 2004). This admits the possibility that species-specific, non-biological factors exist. Our results show that the similarity between the local assemblages depends on the distance between lakes; possibly relating to the colonization processes. Thomaz et al. (2007) recorded that during the flood season some fish species migrate from upper reaches to the floodplain after spawning, and fish communities tend to be more similar among the lakes that comprise a floodplain system. The area hypothesis refers to the existence of a positive relationship between the number of species present in a given area and the size of this area (McArthur & Wilson 1963). Lubinski et al. (2008) verified that lake surface area was one of the most important factors in the structuring of fish communities and local richness (Liu & Wang 2010, Minns 1989, Sondergaard et al. 2005). Larger areas have higher rates of speciation and immigration, and lower rates of extinction. Neotropical freshwater faunas conform well to the species–area relationship (Tedesco et al. 2005). In our study, the local richness manifest significant relationships with the size of the lake and shoreline development, possibly indicating that the dispersal assembly (through hydrological connectivity) is an important ecological factor. A pattern consistently shown in biogeographic studies is a decrease in community similarity with increasing distance between two sampled sites (Qian 2010, Rosindell et al. 2011). This decay is a manifestation of processes controlling community composition that operate across a gradient of scales. Community similarity at large scales tends to decrease environmental similarities, dispersal limitation and niche-width differences (Nekola & White 1999). This relationship obtained suggested that seasonal colonization processes play an important role in fish floodplain assembly. Lakes with a larger surface area comprise greater fish richness than smaller ones, and small lakes contain species with ample regional distribution and abundance. As already shown by Taylor & Warren (2001), species with high local abundances were better colonizers. The regularities observed in our study permit introduction of ecological aspects into the communities in these Neotropical floodplain rivers for purposes of development and planning strategies for biodiversity conservation (Gaston & Blackburn 2000). In order to estimate the total species richness, sampling was designed for each of the various existing habitats. In all the lakes, one sampling station was chosen within each of these four macrohabitats: littoral with trees, littoral without trees, open water, and the connecting channel between the lake and main river. All were sampled simultaneously. Because sampling effort was constant across samples, it was not necessary to adjust richness estimates using rarefaction or other techniques to account for different sampling techniques or sample sizes. The fish were collected using experimental multifilament gillnets, formed from panels measuring 100 × 3 m, in nine different sizes (from 2 to 10 cm stretched mesh). This kind of technique for capture has been used in the studies of associations of fish in oxbow lakes (Winemiller et al. 2000). The nets were set out for 24 h, and checked every 4 h, with the intention of avoiding phenomena such as predators and decomposition due to the high temperature of the water. Fishes were classified as sedentary or short-distance migrant species based on available regional information. Catch per site was standardized according to the length of bank fished and the catch per unit effort (CPUE) determined as fish caught per 100 m. The standardized fish densities were used to calculate basic fish-assemblage metrics, like relative abundance (%) of species and richness. In all analyses for a lake, only the abundances and richness of taxa present at that lake were used. We used the Spearman’s rank correlation coefficient to test the occupancy-abundance relationship. We define the richness of species in a lake as local richness (LR, \( \alpha \)-diversity), and the analysis of all the lakes taken together as regional richness (RR, \( \gamma \)-diversity). We analysed the similarities of assemblages using only presence–absence data. Previous studies have shown that taxonomic patterns may differ when using the presence–absence or abundance data (La Sorte & McKinney 2007). Identification of total phosphate, submerged vegetation cover and zooplankton size thresholds for success of biomanipulation in peri-urban eutrophic ponds Sylvia De Backer · Samuel Teissier · Ludwig Triest Received: 23 November 2012 / Accepted: 27 October 2013 / Published online: 8 November 2013 © Springer Science+Business Media Dordrecht 2013 Abstract In small shallow lakes and ponds, the clear-water state can generally be maintained at higher nutrient concentrations compared to larger shallow lakes. The main objective of this study was to identify thresholds for total phosphorus (TP), submerged vegetation cover and zooplankton size that determine biomanipulation success in peri-urban eutrophic ponds. Additionally, the relationship between transparency and TP is discussed with regard to similar relationships and thresholds reported for shallow lakes. Using classification trees, a threshold TP concentration of 0.300 mg P L\(^{-1}\) was determined below which a clear-water state was generally maintained after biomanipulation. When the average TP concentration was >0.300 mg P L\(^{-1}\), the stability of the clear-water state largely depended on the presence of sufficiently large zooplankton (>0.87 mm) or a submerged vegetation cover of >82% at some point during the year. This threshold TP concentration is considerably higher than the threshold of 0.1 mg L\(^{-1}\) which is generally suggested for longer-term success of biomanipulation in shallow lakes. Such threshold nutrient concentration is important when restoring ecological quality in eutrophic small lakes and ponds. Extended follow-up of biomanipulation success in eutrophic ponds could provide more insight into the feasibility of these thresholds on the longer term. Keywords Ponds · Shallow lakes · Eutrophic · Clear-water state · Restoration · Turbid Introduction During the past decades, ecological quality of shallow lakes and ponds has often been degraded as a result of eutrophication due to human activities, causing a transition to a turbid, phytoplankton-dominated state, often associated with severe blooms of potentially toxic cyanobacteria (Willame et al., 2005; Peretyatko et al., 2007b). Nutrient reduction alone as a method to restore such lakes and ponds is often expensive and inefficient, as recovery is often delayed by internal phosphorus loading or biological resistances (Søndergaard et al., 2005a; Jeppesen et al., 2007). Internal loading was found to be a significant part of total P loading during the productive summer period in eutrophic Danish lakes (Søndergaard et al., 2013). Next to nutrient reduction measures, biomanipulation, through complete or partial fish removal, is often performed to improve ecological quality of shallow lakes (Meijer et al., 1994; Lammens, 1999; Jyväsjärvi et al., 2013). In shallow lakes, a short-term response to biomanipulation is generally dependent on the ability of large zooplankton, once released from its predation pressure, to control phytoplankton sufficiently to create a clear-water state, irrespective of the nutrient levels (van Donk et al., 1990; Meijer et al., 1999). In eutrophic ponds, zooplankton grazing was shown to be a first important mechanism for obtaining a clear-water state (Peretyatko et al., 2009). Once a clear-water state is obtained, the increased water transparency could promote the growth of macrophytes (Bakker et al., 2013) which, in turn, could stabilize the clear-water state on the longer term by a series of mechanisms (Van den Berg et al., 1997; van Donk and van de Bund, 2002; Peretyatko et al., 2007a). On the longer term, however, the success of biomanipulation is more speculative and has often been related to elevated nutrient concentrations (Jeppesen et al., 1990; Søndergaard et al., 2008; Hobbs et al., 2012). The negative relationship between nutrient loading and water transparency in shallow lakes is generally well recognized. Scheffer et al. (1993) already suggested a stepwise rather than a gradual shift from a macrophyte-dominated to a phytoplankton-dominated state when nutrients are gradually increased. Although the theory of only two alternative states has been nuanced lately, the general idea remains that once a certain threshold nutrient concentration is surpassed, a more dramatic increase in turbidity can occur and a return to a clear-water state will be very difficult (Scheffer & van Nes, 2007; Hobbs et al., 2012). Another important factor influencing biomanipulation success in shallow lakes and ponds is the level of nutrients. It is often suggested that the clear-water state in ponds and small lakes is generally less dependent on nutrients compared to larger shallow lakes (Jeppesen et al., 1990; Søndergaard et al., 2005b). In small shallow lakes and ponds, a lower Chlorophyll \( a \) (Chl \( a \)) yield per unit of nitrogen or phosphorus is generally observed (Søndergaard et al., 2005b). Jeppesen et al. (1990) found that ponds (<3 ha) deviated considerably from the overall relationship between water transparency and total phosphorus (TP) in Danish shallow lakes, because both a high transparency and submerged vegetation were still found at higher TP concentrations than for larger lakes. This phenomenon has several possible explanations. Jeppesen et al. (1990) already mentioned that conditions are more favourable for macrophytes in small lakes. Additionally, in smaller lakes and ponds, macrophytes suffer less from wind stress and wind-induced resuspension of the sediment. Also, a reduced depth provides a better light availability for macrophytes at a given water transparency and as such, macrophytes can colonize larger parts of the lake area (Scheffer and van Nes, 2007; Van Geest et al., 2007). Jeppesen et al. (1990) found that for a given shallow lake, transparency was higher when an average submerged vegetation cover of >30% was present, compared to cases with a cover <30%, confirming the positive effect of submerged vegetation on transparency (Scheffer, 1998; van Donk and van de Bund, 2002). Favourable conditions for macrophytes in ponds thus could contribute to an increased transparency, despite high nutrient concentrations. Also, in ponds, some piscivorous fish, such as northern pike (Esox lucius L.), benefit from an abundant vegetation and a higher shore to total area ratio (Grimm, 1989). Winter fish kill due to oxygen depletion could also play a major role, increasing zooplankton grazing during summer, resulting in a more efficient control of phytoplankton (Søndergaard et al., 2005b), which can favour the growth of submerged macrophytes. When biomanipulation is performed on shallow lakes or ponds, it can be useful to determine above which nutrient level a clear-water state can no longer be achieved. When nutrient concentrations (mainly phosphorus) are above a certain threshold, a shift back to the turbid state after biomanipulation might be inevitable and in such cases a nutrient reduction is recommended before biomanipulation is performed. According to Jeppesen et al. (1990), a long-term effect of biomanipulation can only be achieved when the average TP concentration is below 0.1 mg L\(^{-1}\) in shallow lakes larger than 3 ha. Hosper & Jagtman (1990) came to similar conclusions and suggested 0.1 mg L\(^{-1}\) as a threshold for a stable clear-water state after biomanipulation of shallow lakes. In shallow lakes with a TP concentration higher than 0.1 mg L\(^{-1}\), only short-term effects can be expected. Higher nutrient threshold levels could be an advantage for deciding and attempting a restoration of eutrophic ponds through biomanipulation. Nevertheless, even for ponds, beyond a certain threshold, nutrient levels might be too high to obtain a stable clear-water state after fish removal on the longer term. For management purposes, it is crucial to determine the threshold nutrient concentrations above which biomanipulation will no longer be successful in highly eutrophicated ponds. The main objective of this study was to identify thresholds for key factors (TP concentration, submerged vegetation cover and zooplankton size) that are known to strongly determine the outcome of biomanipulation in a series of peri-urban eutrophic ponds. Additionally, the relationships between transparency and TP, and the obtained thresholds for eutrophic ponds are discussed with regard to similar relationships and thresholds reported for shallow lakes. Materials and methods Study area For this study, 13 ponds, located in the Brussels Capital Region (Belgium), were biomanipulated and monitored during 2004–2010. All ponds are located within the same catchment (Woluwe river catchment) in a close proximity of each other (<10 km) and their connectivity is rather high. All the ponds were man-made and created more than a century ago by the damming of small low-order streams (Marlier, 1971). They are shallow (maximum depth 3 m), flat-bottomed and range in surface area from 0.2 to 6 ha and are mainly fed by small rivulets and ground water seepage. Fish communities in the Brussels Capital Region generally consist of species that are typical for Western European fresh waters, such as common carp (Cyprinus carpio carpio L.), northern pike (Esox lucius L.), perch (Perca fluviatilis L.), roach (Rutilus rutilus L.) and tench (Tinca tinca L.) (De Backer et al., 2010). More detailed characteristics of the studied ponds, including an overview of the applied restoration measures for each pond, are given in Table 1. Restoration measures Biomanipulation was performed in 13 ponds during 2005–2009 by water drawdown and complete fish removal (Table 1). This was generally done in winter or early spring to avoid the presence of numerous juvenile fish which could easily escape or survive in the mud for some time. In most ponds, the water level could be lowered manually, due to their artificial nature. During water drawdown, fishermen removed all or as much fish as possible using fishing nets. More than 500 kg of fish per ha was removed in each pond, confirming that all ponds were overstocked with fish before biomanipulation. A few weeks to several months after fish removal, the ponds were slowly refilled through overflow of neighbouring ponds, groundwater seepage or inflow of small rivulets. In a second phase, northern pike (Esox lucius L.) were added in an attempt to stabilize the clear-water state. Addition of piscivores is often performed in an attempt to control planktivorous fish after biomanipulation, allowing large zooplankton to increase grazing pressure on phytoplankton and, as such, further stabilizes the clear-water state (Lammens, 1999; Ha et al., 2013). The individuals that were added in the studied ponds were larger than the 0+ pike that are generally used for this purpose, as the result of 0+ pike additions is often not just temporary (Søndergaard et al., 1997) or the added pike lack piscivory (Skov et al., 2003). In February 2008, only 1+ pikes were added to 10 biomanipulated ponds (Table 1). In February 2010, various densities of 1+, 2+ and 3+ pike (with a size of 20, 30 and 45 cm, respectively) were added into 7 biomanipulated ponds. Sampling and sample processing Samples were taken 1 year before and 1–5 years after biomanipulation during the warm season (May–September) on 3–5 occasions per year. A detailed overview of all sampling occasions is given in Table 2. Except for very small ponds, all samples were taken from a boat. Secchi depth was measured using a 30-cm-diameter disc. In case the Secchi disc was still visible when reaching the pond bottom, Secchi depth was estimated as the actual pond depth plus 1 m in case the disc was still clearly visible or plus 0.1 m in case it was only partially visible. This approach is similar to the method of Cottenie et al. (2001) and was used to obtain a more realistic Secchi depth when the disc was still visible at the pond bottom. Quantitative phytoplankton, Chl \( a \), main nutrient (TP, soluble reactive phosphorus—SRP, and dissolved inorganic nitrogen i.e. \( \mathrm{NH}_4^+ \) and \( \mathrm{NO}_x \) (NO\(_2^-\) and NO\(_3^-\))) and zooplankton samples were collected on each occasion. Mixed water samples based on 10 random subsamples were taken from each pond (including vegetated parts) with a plastic tube sampler of 4.5 cm diameter and 70 cm length that closes in the lower part. An extension was fixed to the sampler to reach the deeper parts of the ponds when appropriate. In case of deeper ponds (depth >1 m), subsamples were taken alternately from shallower and deeper parts of the pond in order to obtain a sample representative of the whole water column. After stirring the collected water, 500 ml was taken for phytoplankton identification and quantification, 1 l for chemical analyses and 1 l for Chl \( a \) determination. Samples for Chl \( a \) analysis were filtered onto Whatman GF/C filters and stored at −18 °C for a maximum of 7 days before analysis. Pigments were extracted in 90% acetone in the dark for 8 h. Pigment concentrations were measured spectrophotometrically. Nutrient concentrations were measured according to standard methods (APHA-AWWA-WEF, 1995). Phytoplankton samples were fixed in the field with alkaline lugol, sodium thiosulphate and buffered formalin (Sherr & Sherr, 1993) and stored in the dark before identification and enumeration to genus level using inverted microscopy. Biovolumes were calculated using the approximations of cell shapes to simple geometrical forms (Wetzel & Likens, 2000). Total phytoplankton biovolume was mainly used as a proxy for turbidity of the water column. Eight phytoplankton groups were differentiated: Cyanobacteria, Bacillariophyta, Euglenophyta, Chlorophyta, Cryptophyta, Dinophyta, Chrysophyta and Xanthophyta. In order to assess the zooplankton community structure, 10 subsamples of 1 l were collected with the same sampler used for phytoplankton and nutrients. Statistical data analyses To identify the factors that determine the outcome of biomanipulation (i.e. ‘failure’ or ‘success’), it is essential to define exactly what ‘failure’ is or what can be considered as ‘success’. In terms of phytoplankton biovolume and composition, ‘failure’ of biomanipulation is essentially a return to a situation that is comparable to the phytoplankton composition and biomass before biomanipulation. Therefore, a hierarchical cluster analysis was performed on averaged per year phytoplankton data (division level). All data were log-transformed to obtain normality if needed. By arranging the data into different clusters, we could study how the situation before biomanipulation was related to the situation after biomanipulation for each pond, in each year. The cluster analysis was performed using PC-ORD (McCune & Mefford, 2006). Sørensen distance was used as a dissimilarity measure and the farthest neighbour linkage as group linkage method. One-way clustering was carried out on both samples and phytoplankton groups. For the latter, data were relativised (i.e. each value divided by the maximum value observed per phytoplankton group). This is generally done to avoid separation of more common species into separate groups from rare species (McCune & Mefford, 2006). Based on previous field observations and the nature of the data, we expect a clustering into two main groups, corresponding to clear with low phytoplankton biomass and to turbid with high phytoplankton biomass conditions. Based on the position of each data point within the cluster, successfully biomanipulated ponds (situation 1), situated inside a low phytoplankton biomass group, could be further subdivided into two categories: before (1b) and after (1a) biomanipulation. Ponds where biomanipulation failed (situation 2) were defined as ponds where data of at least 1 year after biomanipulation were situated inside a high phytoplankton biomass group within the cluster. Situation 2 could be further subdivided into three categories: before biomanipulation (2b), after biomanipulation but before failure (2a, situated in the low phytoplankton subcluster) and after biomanipulation when it failed (2f, data with high phytoplankton biovolume). Essentially, the cluster analysis based on phytoplankton data was performed to assign each data point to one of the 5 predefined categories (1b, 1a, 2b, 2a or 2f). Differences between these 5 categories were analyzed further using One-way ANOVA. A Tukey HSD test, modified for unequal sample size, was used as a post hoc comparison test to compare mean values between individual groups. The one-sample Kolmogorov–Smirnov test was used to investigate the data for normality and the Brown–Forsythe test was used to check for homogeneity of variance. When one of both assumptions was not met (as was the case for SRP and submerged vegetation cover), a non-parametric Kruskal–Wallis test was used to investigate differences between the groups. For all analyses, averaged per year per pond data were used. Three repeated-measures ANOVA were carried out on the considered variables (mean TP, mean phytoplankton biovolume, length of large Cladocera and %SVmax) with time (year) as factor because biomanipulations were not carried out in the same year for every pond. ANOVA was done for the years ‘before biomanipulation’, for the first year following biomanipulation and for all follow-up years after biomanipulation. An additional repeated measure ANOVA was done for the same variables for all ponds in 2010 but using pike addition as a factor in three classes, namely no addition, pikes added in 2008 and pikes added in 2010. Previous research indicated that the impact of total phosphorus concentration (TP), large Cladocera length (LCL) and submerged vegetation cover (SV_{max}) on phytoplankton biovolume in these ponds did not show a linear but a threshold relationship (De Backer, 2011). Therefore, classification trees (Breiman et al., 1984) were used to estimate the thresholds of different environmental factors that determine the outcome of biomanipulation (i.e. phytoplankton biovolume). This type of analysis could allow us to identify threshold values for each predictor (TP, LCL and SV_{max}), below or above which biomanipulation will most likely fail or be successful. All classification tree analyses were performed with Statistica version 8 (Statsoft Inc., Tulsa, OK, USA). The goodness of fit of each split was estimated by the Chi square statistic. Only the best fitting option was shown in the resulting graph. The ‘prune on deviance’ option was used as a stopping rule with a minimum of 10% of the total number of cases needed to allow a subsequent split. For all classification tree analyses, averaged per year per pond values of post-biomanipulation data were used. A series of classification trees was performed to explore the relationships between phytoplankton biovolume and the three predictors (all together or each predictor individually). Since submerged vegetation can affect phytoplankton, phytoplankton can also affect submerged vegetation cover, using average submerged vegetation cover (SV_{av}) as a predictor of phytoplankton biovolume seems irrelevant, as the percentage of cover might be negatively influenced by phytoplankton itself. Use of SV_{max} as a predictor variable of phytoplankton biovolume, rather than SV_{av}, allows us to identify the threshold cover of submerged vegetation above which an increased phytoplankton growth is prevented. Finally, the relationship between phytoplankton biovolume and submerged vegetation cover (SV_{max}), LCL and TP concentration was studied using Pearson product-moment correlations. For all phytoplankton groups (with the exception of Chrysophyta and Xanthophyta that clustered separately from all other groups), the highest phytoplankton biovolume values were found in pond samples of Group B. All pre-biomanipulation samples aggregated into Group B, except for two cases (VKn1 and WtMl). Features of ponds before and after biomanipulation All the ponds studied were rich in nutrients with a mean TP >0.1 mg, before and after biomanipulation. Nutrient levels were generally higher in situations where biomanipulation failed, as TP concentrations were significantly lower in clear-water situations after biomanipulation (1a) when compared to turbid ponds following a failure (2f) (Fig. 2; Table 3). All other TP concentrations were intermediate between those of 1a and 2f. SRP concentrations did not differ significantly between before and after biomanipulation but this is only in cases where biomanipulation was successful (1b and 1a). On the other hand, dissolved nutrients (SRP, NH_4^+ and NO_x) often attained more elevated concentrations after biomanipulation (Fig. 2) and this was significantly higher for SRP in ponds where biomanipulation failed (2f). The five status groups (1b, 1a, 2b, 2a and 2f) showed significant differences in total phytoplankton biovolume, relative cyanobacterial biovolume, Secchi depth, large Cladocera length, %SV_{max} cover and SRP, whereas large Cladocera density was only marginally significant (Table 3, Fig. 2). For NH_4^+ and NO_x concentrations, no significant differences were obtained (Table 3; Fig. 2). The three proxies for phytoplankton biomass (averaged total phytoplankton biovolume, Chl a concentrations and Secchi depth) showed a very similar pattern for the distinguishable situations (Fig. 2; Table 3). Phytoplankton biomass was high in all starting conditions prior to biomanipulation and was comparably high for failed situations of subsequent years (1b, 2b and 2f). Significantly low phytoplankton biomass was measured in situations where biomanipulation was immediately (1a) or temporarily successful (2a). In those situations where biomanipulation temporarily kept a clear-water condition before returning to a turbid state (2a), phytoplankton biovolume also did decrease significantly; however, returned in the following year(s) again to failure (2f) up to a level that was comparable to their origin situation before biomanipulation. Although average relative cyanobacterial biovolume did not differ significantly between most of the situations, it varied considerably in those ponds where biomanipulation failed, namely reaching up to 40% prior to biomanipulation (2b) or when the water shifted to a turbid state again (2f). In temporarily successful conditions (2a), the average relative cyanobacterial biovolume (Fig. 2) could reach up to 20% before turning into failure with higher abundances. In ponds where biomanipulation was successful in maintaining clear-water conditions (1a), the relative cyanobacterial biovolume also was <10% in the period prior to biomanipulation (1b). Determining thresholds of TP, LCL and SVmax needed for successful biomanipulation A first classification tree was performed to differentiate between ponds where biomanipulation failed and ponds where biomanipulation succeeded, based on TP, LCL and SVmax. For this purpose, only data after biomanipulation were used. The classes that were determined for different post-biomanipulation situations were used as a categorical, dependent variable: 1a (after biomanipulation when it was successful, \( N = 31 \)), 2a (after biomanipulation but before failure, \( N = 6 \)) and 2f (when biomanipulation failed, \( N = 11 \)). As such, differences between failure and success situations in the level of TP, LCL or SVmax (added as predictors of the categorical variable) could be identified (Fig. 3). The first split of the resulting tree was based on a TP concentration of 0.300 mg L−1 and separated most of the cases in which biomanipulation was successful (1a) from most of the cases in which biomanipulation failed, both before (2a) and after (2f) failure. 27 out of 30 cases (90%) with an average TP concentration below 0.300 mg L−1 were successfully biomanipulated (1a; Fig. 3; ID = 2). Out of the 18 cases with an average TP concentration of >0.300 mg L−1, 14 cases (78%) are from ponds where biomanipulation failed, before (2a) or after failure (2f; Fig. 3; ID = 3). Thus, a threshold of 0.300 mg L−1 of TP was determined below which biomanipulation is generally successful. When TP >0.300 mg L−1, cases in which biomanipulation has not yet failed (2a) are separated from the cases in which biomanipulation failed (2f) by a larger length (>0.99 mm) of large cladocerans (Fig. 3; ID = 15). Thus, when TP is >0.300 mg L−1, failure of biomanipulation can be prevented as long as cladocerans are sufficiently large (except for one case of ‘2f’ in which LCL is also >0.99 mm). Once LCL decreases to ≤0.99 mm, failure is most likely (Fig. 3; ID = 18). Regarding the % cover of submerged macrophytes that restored after biomanipulation, a threshold of failure in highly eutrophic conditions (TP >0.300 mg L−1) could be considered as 87% of submerged vegetation covering the pond surface (Fig. 3; ID = 16). Next, in order to quantify the difference between failure and success situations in terms of phytoplankton biovolume, a threshold of phytoplankton biovolume was estimated that determines success (1a) or failure (2f). For this purpose, a classification tree was used with the ‘post-biomanipulation status’ (‘1a’, ‘2a’ or ‘2f’) as a response variable and averaged phytoplankton biovolume as a predictor. An almost ‘pure’ split was obtained at 10.8 mm3 L−1 of phytoplankton biovolume, separating all clear-water situations (\( N = 38 \) i.e. ‘1a’: after successful biomanipulation and ‘2a’: before failure) with an average phytoplankton biovolume ≤10.8 mm3 L−1 from all failure situations (2f with \( N = 11 \)) with an average phytoplankton biovolume of >10.8 mm3 L−1 (except Fig. 3 Classification tree for three categories of after biomanipulation situations: 1a—successfully biomanipulated ponds after biomanipulation; 2a, 2f—unsuccessfully biomanipulated ponds after biomanipulation: before and after failure, for one case of 2f with a low phytoplankton biovolume). The obtained threshold of 10.8 mm\(^3\) L\(^{-1}\) of phytoplankton biovolume was then used in further analyses to differentiate between clear-water and turbid situations. Based on this threshold, 2 categories were created: categories ‘0’ and ‘1’ for cases in which phytoplankton biovolume was \( \leq \) or \( > \) than the threshold biovolume of 10.8 mm\(^3\) L\(^{-1}\), respectively. For all remaining analyses, the phytoplankton data were transformed to ‘0’ or ‘1’ values and used as such instead of the original phytoplankton data. These two categories of phytoplankton biovolume were then used in further analyses. Using all three predictors in the same analysis might blur the effect of some predictors individually on phytoplankton biovolume. Therefore, the classification tree analysis based on these two phytoplankton categories was executed with TP, LCL or SV\(_{\text{max}}\) individually as categorical predictors to study the behaviour of phytoplankton depending on each respectively. Averaged per year TP, averaged large Cladocera length (LCL) and maximum submerged vegetation cover (SV) were used as continuous predictors of biomanipulation category. Above 0.300 mg P L\(^{-1}\), both categories of phytoplankton biovolume could occur (Fig. 4a; ID = 3). Discussion On the short term, a clear-water state can be established in ponds after biomanipulation, independent of the level of nutrients. The likelihood of obtaining such a clear-water state depends mostly on the development of sufficiently large cladocerans after biomanipulation, irrespective of the nutrient levels present (Peretyatko et al., 2009). On the longer term, nutrients will play a more important role in determining biomanipulation success. Biomanipulated ponds with a TP concentration below 0.300 mg P L\(^{-1}\) resided in a clear-water state with low phytoplankton biomass, relatively independent of large cladoceran size or the extent of submerged vegetation cover (except for one case without submerged vegetation Fig. 5 Relationship between phytoplankton biovolume and TP, large Cladocera length (LCL) and maximum submerged vegetation cover (SV_{max}) when TP \leq 0.300\ \mathrm{mg\ P\ L}^{-1} (left) or >0.300\ \mathrm{mg\ P\ L}^{-1} (right) in ponds after biomanipulation. Significant Pearson correlations (\( P < 0.05 \)) are indicated by a line; for the lower two graphs, a dotted line corresponds to all cases with LCL \leq 0.87; a full line corresponds to all cases with LCL >0.87. More details concerning the Pearson correlations are given in Table 4 and where large cladoceran length is <0.83 mm). Above 0.300 mg P L^{-1}, the maintenance of the clear-water state mainly depended on large Cladocera size. As long as sufficiently large cladocerans were present (average length >0.87 mm), phytoplankton biomass remained low, even at high TP concentrations. If, however, in such case, large Cladocera size decreased due to predation by recolonizing fish (De Backer et al., 2012), a shift to the turbid state was unavoidable, except for a few cases in which submerged vegetation cover reached >82% and where a clear-water state was maintained despite the lack of sufficiently large cladocerans. Despite the often high cover of submerged vegetation that was often observed in spring, several ponds still developed a high phytoplankton biomass in summer and, nevertheless, returned to a turbid state. Long-term follow-up of these ponds could clarify if this is only a transitional stage to a permanent turbid state where macrophyte cover will eventually be absent, even in spring. Failure of biomanipulation thus appears to be related mainly to a combination of both elevated nutrient concentrations and the lack of large Cladocera grazing, independently of the extent of the submerged vegetation cover. After biomanipulation, all ponds remained in a clear-water state below 0.300 mg L\(^{-1}\) of TP, independent of the extent of the submerged vegetation cover. It should, however, be noted that in biomanipulated ponds, in most of the ponds with an average TP concentration <0.300 mg L\(^{-1}\), LCL was >0.87 mm, which could have been the main reason for low phytoplankton biomass below 0.300 mg L\(^{-1}\) of TP. Although the positive effect of large zooplankton grazing and the presence of submerged vegetation is generally well recognized (Van den Berg et al., 1997; Scheffer, 1998; van Donk and van de Bund, 2002), few studies have shown the direct impact of these factors on Chl \(a\)--TP relationships in shallow lakes or ponds. Chl \(a\)--TP relationships were studied in the same 13 biomanipulated ponds, showing that after biomanipulation, for a given TP concentration, the yield of Chl \(a\) was lower in ponds with an extensive submerged vegetation cover and high grazing pressure, compared to the same ponds before biomanipulation (Teissier et al., 2012). This directly shows that other factors than nutrients, such as submerged vegetation cover and large zooplankton grazing, can considerably influence the Chl \(a\)--TP relationship in eutrophic ponds. An additional difference between the situation before biomanipulation and during the first years after biomanipulation is the presence of large benthivorous fish in the former. Benthivorous fish that resuspend the sediment, thereby increasing suspended solids, nutrients and phytoplankton abundance in the water column, can cause a reduction of transparency and prevent macrophyte recolonization (Roozen et al., 2007). Next to the effect of planktivorous fish removal on zooplankton grazing, removal of benthivorous fish also contributes to an increased sedimentation and an improved transparency after biomanipulation (Meijer et al., 1990). This aspect could also have contributed to the lower Chl \(a\)--TP yield in biomanipulated ponds. As in several ponds, fish recolonized after biomanipulation, large benthivorous fish might eventually be present again in these ponds. We did not observe any significant improvement on large zooplankton density or length in 2010 in any of the ponds in which pike were added. Therefore, it is unlikely that the numbers of pike that survived were sufficient to reduce predation pressure on zooplankton in any pond in 2010. In a similar study on non-biomanipulated ponds (De Backer, 2011), no clear-water state is found when TP is >0.300 mg L\(^{-1}\). Therefore, it also is unlikely that biomanipulated ponds with an average TP concentration above this threshold will remain clear in the future (if biomanipulation did not already fail). Consequently, nutrient reduction is recommended before biomanipulation when average TP concentrations exceed the threshold concentration of \( \sim 0.300 \) mg L\(^{-1}\). It is often suggested that in smaller lakes and ponds, phytoplankton is less influenced by nutrients (Jeppesen et al., 1990) and that factors other than nutrients are more important for phytoplankton control (Søndergaard et al., 2005b; Peretyatko et al., 2007b). Our results confirm this, although the threshold levels obtained should be interpreted carefully due to limited number of data and additionally need to be validated with an additional training set using non-biomanipulated ponds. The threshold TP concentration of \( \sim 0.300 \) mg P L\(^{-1}\) below which a clear-water state can be maintained is considerably higher than the threshold of 0.1–0.125 mg P L\(^{-1}\) that is often suggested for shallow lakes (Hosper & Jagtman, 1990; Jeppesen et al., 1990). As already mentioned, high submerged vegetation cover and large zooplankton grazing can considerably influence the Chl \(a\)--TP relationship in eutrophic ponds. Possibly, the strong effect of both factors can be the reason for the lesser dependence of phytoplankton biomass on nutrients in ponds, compared to shallow lakes. Similar studies on shallow lakes could demonstrate whether the effect of zooplankton grazing and submerged vegetation on the Chl \(a\)--TP relationship would be as strong as it is in the case of the pond systems studied here. Conclusions For biomanipulation of eutrophic ponds, our results suggest that, although a clear-water state can be obtained even when TP concentrations are >0.300 mg P L\(^{-1}\), the stability of this clear-water state is insufficient and largely depends on the presence of sufficiently large-sized zooplankton or of a nearly full cover of submerged vegetation. Once they disappear, generally through predation or disturbance by recolonizing fish, a shift to the turbid state is very likely. As fish recolonization is almost inevitable at some point in these peri-urban ponds (or at least difficult to avoid in the near proximity of recreational fishing areas), we suggest that nutrient reduction measures should be undertaken before biomanipulation, in case the average TP concentration is >0.300 mg P L\(^{-1}\). After 2–4 years following biomanipulation, all biomanipulated ponds with a TP concentration below this threshold showed promising results, as they remained in a clear-water state during the whole study period. Longer term studies on biomanipulated ponds are necessary to see how the situation in these ponds will evolve. The threshold concentration of 0.300 mg L\(^{-1}\) of TP above which biomanipulation is likely to fail is considerably higher than similar thresholds known for shallow lakes. Such lesser dependence of phytoplankton biomass in the studied biomanipulated ponds could be caused by the strong effect of large zooplankton grazing and submerged vegetation cover on phytoplankton biomass in eutrophic ponds. Higher nutrient threshold levels could be an advantage for deciding and attempting a restoration of eutrophic ponds through biomanipulation. Nevertheless, even for ponds, beyond a certain threshold, nutrient levels might be too high to obtain a stable clear-water state after fish removal on the longer term. For management purposes, it is crucial to determine the threshold nutrient concentrations above which biomanipulation will no longer be successful in highly eutrophicated ponds. The main objective of this study was to identify thresholds for key factors (TP concentration, submerged vegetation cover and zooplankton size) that are known to strongly determine the outcome of biomanipulation in a series of peri-urban eutrophic ponds. Additionally, the relationships between transparency and TP, and the obtained thresholds for eutrophic ponds are discussed with regard to similar relationships and thresholds reported for shallow lakes. Materials and methods Study area For this study, 13 ponds, located in the Brussels Capital Region (Belgium), were biomanipulated and monitored during 2004–2010. All ponds are located within the same catchment (Woluwe river catchment) in a close proximity of each other (<10 km) and their connectivity is rather high. All the ponds were man-made and created more than a century ago by the damming of small low-order streams (Marlier, 1971). They are shallow (maximum depth 3 m), flat-bottomed and range in surface area from 0.2 to 6 ha and are mainly fed by small rivulets and ground water seepage. Fish communities in the Brussels Capital Region generally consist of species that are typical for Western European fresh waters, such as common carp (Cyprinus carpio carpio L.), northern pike (Esox lucius L.), perch (Perca fluviatilis L.), roach (Rutilus

In situations where biomanipulation failed (2f), the average submerged vegetation cover was not significantly lower compared to the clear-water situations after biomanipulation (1a and 2a). The variation in submerged vegetation cover after biomanipulation failure was still high, ranging from 0 to more than 60%. It should be noted that a high macrophyte cover in failure situations (2f) was generally observed in late spring, before the development of high phytoplankton biovolume in mid-summer, after which macrophytes generally disappeared. Determining thresholds of TP, LCL and SVmax needed for successful biomanipulation A first classification tree was performed to differentiate between ponds where biomanipulation failed and ponds where biomanipulation succeeded, based on TP, LCL and SVmax. For this purpose, only data after biomanipulation were used. The classes that were determined for different post-biomanipulation situations were used as a categorical, dependent variable: 1a (after biomanipulation when it was successful, \( N = 31 \)), 2a (after biomanipulation but before failure, \( N = 6 \)) and 2f (when biomanipulation failed, \( N = 11 \)). As such, differences between failure and success situations in the level of TP, LCL or SVmax (added as predictors of the categorical variable) could be identified (Fig. 3). The first split of the resulting tree was based on a TP concentration of 0.300 mg L−1 and separated most of the cases in which biomanipulation was successful (1a) from most of the cases in which biomanipulation failed, both before (2a) and after (2f) failure. 27 out of 30 cases (90%) with an average TP concentration below 0.300 mg L−1 were successfully biomanipulated (1a; Fig. 3; ID = 2). Out of the 18 cases with an average TP concentration of >0.300 mg L−1, 14 cases (78%) are from ponds where biomanipulation failed, before (2a) or after failure (2f; Fig. 3; ID = 3). Thus, a threshold of 0.300 mg L−1 of TP was determined below which biomanipulation is generally successful. When TP >0.300 mg L−1, cases in which biomanipulation has not yet failed (2a) are separated from the cases in which biomanipulation failed (2f) by a larger length (>0.99 mm) of large cladocerans (Fig. 3; ID = 15). Thus, when TP is >0.300 mg L−1, failure of biomanipulation can be prevented as long as cladocerans are sufficiently large (except for one case of ‘2f’ in which LCL is also >0.99 mm). Once LCL decreases to ≤0.99 mm, failure is most likely (Fig. 3; ID = 18). Regarding the % cover of submerged macrophytes that restored after biomanipulation, a threshold of failure in highly eutrophic conditions (TP >0.300 mg L−1) could be considered as 87% of submerged vegetation covering the pond surface (Fig. 3; ID = 16). Next, in order to quantify the difference between failure and success situations in terms of phytoplankton biovolume, a threshold of phytoplankton biovolume was estimated that determines success (1a) or failure (2f). For this purpose, a classification tree was used with the ‘post-biomanipulation status’ (‘1a’, ‘2a’ or ‘2f’) as a response variable and averaged phytoplankton biovolume as a predictor. Lake metabolism scales with lake morphometry and catchment conditions Peter A. Staehr · Lars Baastrup-Spohr · Kaj Sand-Jensen · Colin Stedmon Received: 21 January 2011 / Accepted: 2 May 2011 / Published online: 17 May 2011 © Springer Basel AG 2011 Abstract We used a comparative data set for 25 lakes in Denmark sampled during summer to explore the influence of lake morphometry, catchment conditions, light availability and nutrient input on lake metabolism. We found that (1) gross primary production (GPP) and community respiration (R) decline with lake area, water depth and drainage ratio, and increase with algal biomass (Chl), dissolved organic carbon (DOC) and total phosphorus (TP); (2) all lakes, especially small with less incident light, and forest lakes with high DOC, have negative net ecosystem production (NEP < 0); (3) daily variability of GPP decreases with lake area and water depth as a consequence of lower input of nutrients and organic matter per unit water volume; (4) the influence of benthic processes on free water metabolic measures declines with increasing lake size; and (5) with increasing lake size, lake metabolism decreases significantly per unit water volume, while depth integrated areal rates remain more constant due to a combination of increased light and nutrient limitation. Overall, these meta-parameters have as many significant but usually weaker relationships to whole-lake and benthic metabolism as have TP, Chl and DOC that are directly linked to photosynthesis and respiration. Combining water depth and Chl to predict GPP, and water depth and DOC to predict R, lead to stronger multiple regression models accounting for 57–63% of the variability of metabolism among the 25 lakes. It is therefore important to consider differences in lake morphometry and catchment conditions when comparing metabolic responses of lakes to human impacts. Keywords Lake metabolism · Lake morphometry · Catchment conditions · Intrinsic drivers · Temporal variability Introduction Research on lake metabolism has shown that gross primary production (GPP), respiration (R) and net ecosystem production (NEP = GPP – R) vary considerably among lakes and over time within lakes (Cole et al. 2000; Hanson et al. 2006; Staehr and Sand-Jensen 2007; Staehr et al. 2010a). Many lakes have a negative NEP and most release CO₂ to the atmosphere. This is due to the considerable supply and substantial degradation of allochthonous organic material from the surrounding landscape (Sand-Jensen and Staehr 2007, 2009). While day-to-day differences in metabolism within a lake are primarily driven by changes in light, temperature and vertical mixing (Hanson et al. 2006; Staehr and Sand-Jensen 2007), long-term differences in metabolism between lakes are strongly related to changes in concentrations of total phosphorus (TP), phytoplankton chlorophyll (Chl) and dissolved organic carbon (DOC) (Sand-Jensen and Staehr 2007, 2009). Thus, autotrophic lakes (NEP > 0) typically have high TP, high Chl and low DOC concentrations, whereas the most heterotrophic lakes have low TP, low Chl and high DOC (Hanson et al. 2003; Sand-Jensen and Staehr 2007). Lake morphometry (surface area and depth), catchment properties (geology, size and land use) and hydrology have a strong influence on lake temperature, physical mixing, nutrient concentrations, DOC, Chl and transparency (Fee et al. 1996; Hanson et al. 2007; Nõges 2009), suggesting that these conditions operate as meta-parameters with an indirect but potentially strong effect on lake metabolism. Implicit scaling of lake productivity to lake size has been considered for decades (Thienemann 1927; Brylinsky and Mann 1973; Fee et al. 1992), and location in forests or open landscapes is also known to affect metabolism (Tranvik 1992; del Giorgio and Peters 1994; Sand-Jensen and Staehr 2007, 2009). Thus, lake area is statistically positively related to wind exposure, water depth and mixing depth and inversely related to external input of nutrients and DOC per water volume and surface area (e.g., Brylinsky and Mann 1973; Duarte and Kalff 1989; Fee et al. 1996). Drainage ratio (catchment area:lake area) is positively related to external input of nutrients, CO\(_2\) and DOC (Gergel et al. 1999). Forest cover is negatively correlated with nutrient input and incoming irradiance for small lakes and positively correlated with DOC input and light attenuation by coloured DOC (Xenopoulos et al. 2003; Sand-Jensen and Staehr 2007). In contrast to the substantial literature on the importance of meta-parameters for lake chemistry and physics, there are few comparative measurements of whole-lake metabolism, for a sufficiently large number of lakes, to evaluate the importance of lake size and catchment conditions on whole-lake metabolism and atmospheric CO\(_2\) exchange. This study investigates the effect of these meta-parameters on GPP, R and NEP, and compares their role with that of traditional direct drivers of metabolism (i.e., Chl, DOC, light and temperature). Our general expectation is that meta-parameters are significant though probably not as strong predictors of GPP, R and NEP as the intrinsic variables directly involved in metabolic processes. If so, more general predictive models can be derived and new understanding of control mechanisms can be obtained. Our first specific prediction is that both volumetric GPP and R should decline with increasing lake area, water depth and drainage ratio, as the concentrations and input of nutrients and DOC decrease (Nõges 2009). Although light availability decreases with increasing depth of the photic zone, light availability, is, however, expected to be similar across lake sizes as lower inputs of light absorbing material and greater mixing depth in larger lakes should cause mean light availability to remain similar among lakes of different sizes. Areal rates of GPP integrated over the entire water column is therefore expected to vary little with lake size, and the influence of lake size for GPP expected to be higher for volume specific rates. Our second specific prediction is that small lakes should have higher DOC input and concentrations and be more net heterotrophic (NEP < 0) than large lakes and that forest lakes should be more net heterotrophic than lakes in open landscapes. Small lakes have a greater contact and possibility of exchange of organic material with the terrestrial landscape along its periphery relative to lake surface area than large lakes. Forest lakes have a direct transfer of litter from the surrounding tree vegetation, receive less light for photosynthesis on the lake surface and have higher DOC concentrations in the water column competing with photosynthetic pigments for available photons causing mean light availability to remain low despite of a shallow mixed depth (Staehr et al. 2010a). Conversely, reduced input of DOC in larger lakes should favour positive NEP as mean light availability for primary production is the same but less allochthonous material is supplied for bacterial oxygen consumption. A final mechanism may restrict benthic photosynthesis relative to respiration in small forest lakes, namely the typical organic-rich sediments of flocculated humic material of low mass density that is physically instable for microalgae and unfavourable for growth of rooted plants (Barko and Smart 1986; Sand-Jensen et al. 2005). Our third specific prediction is that the contribution of benthic processes to whole-lake metabolism declines with increasing water depth. Because light penetration to sediments decreases with water depth, the benthic primary production should be more constrained by water depth than respiration and this should be particularly so in forest lakes with high DOC concentrations and poor light conditions. To the extent that lake depth and lake area are correlated, the role of benthic processes should also decline with increasing lake area, while surrounding forest vegetation may stimulate benthic R but impede GPP and NEP. Our fourth specific prediction is that the day-to-day variability of lake metabolism should decline with increasing lake area and depth. Measurements of whole-lake metabolism were performed over 1 week in each lake for subsequent comparison among all 25 lakes. This duration permits reliable calculations of mean daily metabolism and mean values for other physical, chemical and biological properties (Hanson et al. 2003; Staehr and Sand-Jensen 2007). Moreover, 1 week measurements permit calculation of daily variability of metabolic parameters and their relationship to meta-parameters and within-lake parameters. With increasing lake area and water depth, temporal variations in the magnitude of physical mixing affecting different pelagic populations are likely to decline. Reduced external input of nutrients and DOC per unit water volume with increasing lake size should also reduce the carrying capacity for phytoplankton, zooplankton, bacteria and fish per unit volume and, thereby, dampen population changes and blooms. Materials and methods Study sites We studied lake metabolism in relation to physical, chemical and biological characteristics for about 1 week (6–8 days) in 25 medium to high alkaline lakes during May and June 2007. Systems ranged from ponds (0.1 ha) to midsized (1,729 ha) lakes, and were all located in calcareous moraines in Denmark (Table 1). Lakes were sampled in a random order to avoid bias from changing meteorological conditions during the study. Throughout the study, meteorological conditions were measured from a buoy placed on Lake Slotssø. Daily average wind speed (0.3–5.4 m s\(^{-1}\), min–max) and solar irradiance (5–55 mol photons m\(^{-2}\) day\(^{-1}\)) showed large daily variability, but did not change significantly during the course of the study. Lakes were chosen to cover large ranges in lake size, forest cover, TP, Chl and DOC concentrations. Lake area, catchment area, %forest cover in the catchment and drainage ratio (catchment area:lake area) were obtained for each lake using the digital Areal Information System (Nielsen et al. 2000). To evaluate effects of forest cover on local wind and light conditions, we also determined the proportion of forest in the 200 m wide riparian zone around the lakes from aerial photographs. Limnological variables Triplicate water samples were collected once from each lake as a depth integrated sample from the upper mixed layer at the center between 10 and 12 o’clock. Samples were analyzed for chlorophyll a, DOC, nutrients, alkalinity and pH. Samples for Chl and phaeopigments were filtered through Advantec\textregistered{} GC-50 filters, extracted in 96% ethanol for 24 h and measured according to Jespersen and Christoffersen (1987) using a Shimadzu UV-160A spectrophotometer. Absorbance of colored dissolved organic matter (CDOM) was measured in a GF/F filtrate (0.7 µm) at 300, 340, 360 and 400 nm in a 5 cm cuvette. DOC concentrations (mg C L\(^{-1}\)) were estimated from the linear relationship to CDOM absorption at 360 nm (m\(^{-1}\)): \( \text{DOC} = 0.454 \text{CDOM}_{360} + 1.9 \) (\( r^2 = 0.80 \)) found in a study of 399 water samples from Danish lakes and streams (C. Stedmon, unpubl. data). Total phosphorus (TP) was determined for unfiltered samples by persulfate digestion according to Eaton et al. (1995) and assayed according to Kragh and Sondergaard (2004). Water for determination of pH, alkalinity and CO\(_2\) was transferred to closed, dark glass bottles to avoid CO\(_2\) exchange with the air and prevent photosynthesis before measurement in the laboratory within 2 h. The pH was measured with Radiometer equipment (accuracy 0.01 pH unit). Acidimetric titration of alkalinity (acid neutralizing capacity, ANC), ionic strength, pH and temperature were used to calculate concentrations of free CO\(_2\) according to Rebsdorf (1972). The calculated CO\(_2\) concentrations have previously been shown to be in close agreement with direct CO\(_2\) measurements on an IRGA using a headspace equilibration technique (Sand-Jensen and Frost-Christensen 1998). Fluorescence of DOC was measured on a Varian Eclipse fluorescence spectrophotometer. An emission spectrum was measured every 2 nm between 300 and 600 nm, whilst exciting at 370 nm. The fluorescence index (FI; McKnight et al. 2001) was derived by taking the ratio of the fluorescence at 450 to that at 500 nm. This index can be used to characterize the chemical composition of DOC and indicate the relative contribution of terrestrial and aquatic organic matter. Index values typically range between 1 and 2, with terrestrial plant material resulting in low values. Depth profiles of oxygen and temperature were recorded in situ by an YSI 600XL multisonde. The vertical light attenuation coefficient (K\(_D\), 400–700 nm) was determined from the depth profile of photosynthetically active radiation (PAR) using a LiCor 4π sensor. K\(_D\) was calculated as the slope of a linear regression model of irradiance (E\(_z\)) versus depth (z): \( \ln(E_z) = b + K_D \ z \). Physics and metabolism from sonde measurements We deployed a buoy at the centre of each lake to measure surface PAR, wind speed, water temperature and dissolved oxygen concentration (DO) for about 1 week. Three sets of this equipment were moved between lakes in a random order. Surface PAR was measured 1 m above the surface using a HOBO 2π quantum sensor. Wind speed was measured 1.2 m above the lake using a HOBO anemometer. Surface PAR and wind speed at the centre of each lake were normalized to measurements made throughout the summer in medium-sized Lake Slotssø (22 ha, 15% forest cover; Table 1). Normalization was simply the ratio of the wind speed at a lake to that of Lake Slotssø. This permitted comparison among the 25 lakes despite changes in mean weekly wind velocity and surface PAR during the summer. Water temperature was measured every 10 min during buoy deployment at several water depths, using a string of Stow Away Tidbit loggers. These data permitted calculation of mixing depth (Z\(_\text{mix}\)) at high frequency according to an empirical curve-fitting procedure (Staehr et al. 2010a). Dissolved oxygen was measured at 0.5 m either with an Oxyguard DO sensor or a YSI 600XL multisonde. Oxygen sensors were cleaned and calibrated prior and after each application. Electrode drift was small and was corrected for assuming it is linear over time. Oxygen concentrations recorded every 10 min were used to calculate NEP for 30 min intervals, according to the guidelines presented in Staehr et al.
