Comparable data of pesticide contamination in LSWB are scarce but concentrations from LSWB in the eastern part of Germany, in Brandenburg, can be used for comparison. For metazachlor, in four of ten samples concentrations of 0.764 \( \mu \)g L\(^{-1} \) up to 10.24 \( \mu \)g L\(^{-1} \) were measured in autumns 2012/3. Flufenacet data for comparison are not available since either it was not included in the analytical spectrum of the study or values were below the LOQ (LELF, 2014). The results of metazachlor findings in our study are considerably lower than in the other study. 5. Conclusion The key findings of the study indicate a high temporal and spatial variability in the inputs of the herbicides metazachlor, flufenacet and their TPs into the LSWB. Few similar transport patterns were observed for metazachlor, but not for flufenacet. Despite of closely resembling hydrological data and site characteristics such as soil type, humic content and slope, a considerable spatial heterogeneity is displayed by the almost unique kind of pesticide concentrations in the LSWB over time. The transformation of the mother compounds showed correspondences in the manner of highest TP concentrations in the last sample of the campaign, but TP concentrations varied in the intermediate samples. The TPs of the mother compound applied in the previous year were clearly detected in the following year. This applies in particular for metazachlor-ESA which can be assessed as a permanent exposure in each water body of the study. The analysis of the target compounds' physicochemical properties reveal that the TPs, especially the ESA-TPs, have a higher mobility and persistence than the mother compounds metazachlor and flufenacet. Metazachlor-ESA was detected in almost every sample, even one or two years after application of the mother compound. In contrast, the mother compounds were only measured after application due to their lower DT\(_{50}\). Further results indicate that hydrological parameters are more relevant for pesticide transport than properties of the pesticides or the site characteristics. The rainfall amount and patterns strongly influence the transport of the pesticides. Thereby, the rainfall following application seems to be of higher importance than the antecedent rainfall which effects the initial soil water content. The recording of the water level changes in 2016 clearly demonstrate that the transport of water and hence, of pesticides into LSWB is strongly related to inflow via subsurface flow and becomes apparent to be of high relevance. The target screenings after spring application reveal findings of the pesticides metolachlor, terbuthylazine and its TP desethylatrazine in each LSWB, which may originate from former applications in larger distance. Furthermore, the site characteristics do not explain sufficiently the variations of the concentrations. The same applies for the correlation between physicochemical properties of the water samples such as pH, oxygen content, redox potential and the concentrations of the target compounds. Small-scale characteristics such as subsurface transport via lateral flow and interaction with the shallow groundwater as well as soil moisture or date of application seem to be of higher relevance for pesticide transport. Lentic small water bodies are of major importance for biodiversity but have a high potential to be harmed by agrochemicals due to their location in agricultural fields. The driving factor controlling the transport of pesticides into the LSWB is the precipitation and related to this, the inflow of water and dissolved pesticides. Moreover, the transport how and from where the pesticides enter the LSWB as well as the importance of interactions with the sediments as potential permanent pesticide releaser need to be elucidated. Since studies reveal atmospheric pesticide inputs into surface water bodies, their concentrations in wet and dry depositions should be considered as well. The data base of pesticide contamination of LSWB has definitely to be enlarged by event-based sampling to get a realistic assessment of their exposure. But in addition, continuous long-term monitoring in high temporal resolution e.g. in daily intervals is essential to recognize the processes responsible for pesticide transport at this scale. Without understanding these processes, an efficient protection of the LSWB cannot be achieved as stated in directives, guidelines and national action plans. Hence, there is an urgent need to fill the knowledge gaps to meet the environmental goals in the near future. 3.2. Physicochemical parameters of water samples The physicochemical parameters determined in the field show common values of surface water bodies (Fig. 3). The oxygen concentration was in the range of 1.86–12.74 mg L⁻¹, the temperature in the range of 0.4–18.4 °C (not displayed), the conductivity in the range of 151–664 μS cm⁻¹, the pH value in the range of 6.66–8.52 and the redox potential in the range of 45–259 mV. 3.3. Water levels in the LSWB in autumn 2016 The water levels in relation to the initial water level in the LSWB are displayed in Fig. 4. As demonstrated in Table 4, the precipitation between application and sampling varied among the LSWB. The group of LSWB A2, A4, A6, A9 and A10 were sampled at the same dates and precipitation sums were identical, the changes of the water level varied considerably. As a second group, A5 and A8 were sampled and showed decreasing/slightly increasing water levels which may be related to the lower amount of precipitation in comparison to the other LSWB. The unintended extraction of the rods led to missing values in these LSWB. A7 had again a different sampling scheme due to the late date of application. Overall, the sum of precipitation was almost 20 mm lower than for the other LSWB but the increase of the water level is the second highest increase of all LSWB. 4. Results and discussion of pesticide analyses 4.1. Pesticide target screening after spring application The analyses showed that from the measured 108 compounds, ten compounds in 2015 and twelve compounds in 2016 were quantified above the LOQ (Fig. 5). Most of the compounds with positive findings were detected in one or few LSWB, but metolachlor, terbuthylazine and its TP desethylterbuthylazine were found in each LSWB. Comparing both years, azoxystrobin, cyproconazole, diflufenican were measured solely in 2016, while pirimicarb was found only in 2015. The pesticide concentrations in 2015 were close to the LOQ with four exemptions clearly above 0.1 μg L⁻¹. In 2016, seven findings were higher than 0.1 μg L⁻¹. The highest detected concentration after the spring application was 0.63 μg metolachlor L⁻¹ in A10. Multiple-pesticide contaminations from 3 to 7 compounds were observed in the single LSWB whereas the number of contaminants increased from 2015 to 2016. The highest number of compounds was observed in A7 with 6 compounds in 2015 and 7 compounds in 2016. Due to their high uncertainty, the values of methyldesphenylchloridazone were not considered. Within the twelve compounds detected in concentrations higher than the LOQ, there are four herbicides, three fungicides, three insecticides and two TP of herbicides. Their properties vary concerning mobility and persistence in a broad range (PPDB, 2017, Lewis et al., 2016;) so that inputs cannot be addressed to certain physicochemical characteristics. Considering the land use, none of these compounds had been applied in that year directly to the fields in which the LSWB were located as the crops grown there did not require them. However, in all cases these pesticides had been applied to the crops on either one of the neighbouring fields that year or in autumn/spring of the previous year to the LSWB field. Hence, the pesticide inputs may originate from these adjacent fields or former applications. Exemplarily, diflufenican is a herbicide which is applied in autumn and is part of a widely distributed product. In autumn 2015, this product was applied to field A7 (winter grain) so that the measured concentration in A7 in spring 2016 may result from that application. The same product was applied to A1, A3, A6 and A10 as well in 2015, but residues in July 2016 were not found. These results may lead to the assumption that A7 is more susceptible to pesticide inputs than the other LSWB of the study. The key results of the target screenings are that (i) metolachlor, terbuthylazine and its TP desethyltriazine were found in all LSWB and that (ii) the concentrations of the twelve compounds were lower in 2015 than in 2016. (i) Metolachlor and terbuthylazine are herbicides which are applied to corn. However, they were neither applied in 2015 nor in 2016 and often not for years to the fields of the ten LSWB. In most of the LSWB, the three compounds were detected in both years in background concentrations.01–0.03 μg L⁻¹. In 2016 in A10, 0.315 μg L⁻¹ terbuthylazine and 0.63 μg L⁻¹ metolachlor were found. Since a field with corn cultivation in 2016 is next to A10, it can be assumed that these concentrations are caused by the release from this field to A10. There were no further fields with corn cultivation close to the other LSWB which could explain the findings of terbuthylazine and metolachlor. Sandin et al. Lischeid et al. (2017) observed natural ponds to identify external drivers of their water quality. The results obtained reveal that size and location of the ponds' catchment is of crucial importance and that it is often related to shallow groundwater systems. Especially at small scale and without flowing water bodies, topography and groundwater levels are not sufficient for the delineation. Lischeid et al. (2017) showed that subsurface catchments of these LSWB can exceed sizes of 2 ha. In consequence, the residence time of dissolved compounds such as pesticides in subsurface flow can be high. Sandin et al. (2018) explained their findings of formerly applied pesticides by intermittent transport processes which relocate the pesticides to the subsoil where degradation is slower than in topsoil. In the subsoil, pesticides can be stored and slowly released so that they cause a signal over a long period. The results of these two studies explain that the corn-herbicide findings in our LSWB may originate via hydraulic subsurface connection and slow transport in the subsoil from former applications in larger distance.

(ii) To explain the concentration differences between the years, the amount and distribution of the precipitation from 1st April to 5th July were compared. The precipitation sum was 149 mm in 2015 and 299 mm in 2016 in 8 km distance, and 169 mm (2015) and 214 mm (2016) in 2–4 km distance. The overall amount of rainfall was clearly higher in 2016 than in 2015. The distribution shows higher rainfall amounts in April and June in 2016, but higher ones in May 2015. In general, the herbicides metolachlor and terbuthylazine are applied to corn in May while the fungicide tebuconazole is applied to rape in April/May and to grain from April to middle of June. The higher precipitation in 2016 caused a more frequent application of tebuconazole than in 2015: six of eight fields were sprayed in 2016, while in 2015, two of five fields were sprayed. Two rainfall events of 30–50 mm at the end of June 2016 may have caused enhanced relocation especially of metolachlor, tebuconazole and terbuthylazine. According to their properties (water solubility, log P, Kfoc, DT50 soil) (PPDB, 2017, Lewis et al., 2016), they are assessed to be moderately mobile and moderately or non-persistent so that a higher potential for discharge cannot be derived. Hence, the combination of the rainfall pattern and the time of application may have caused the differences of pesticide findings in 2015 and 2016.

4.2. Analyses of metazachlor, flufenacet and their TPs in autumn samples 2015 and 2016

4.2.1. Transport and transformation of metazachlor in LSWB located in rape fields

Five LSWB were monitored in 2015 for metazachlor and its TP concentrations. Metazachlor was not detected in concentrations higher than LOQ before application (Fig. 6). After application, the maximum concentration amounted to 0.62 \( \mu \)g L\(^{-1}\) in A8 after the second rainfall event. The following observations were made: In all 5 LSWB, metazachlor concentrations were highest after the 1st rainfall event following the application. Over time, the concentrations decreased. We assessed this as prevalent patterns. However, the reduction of concentration varies between the LSWB from 20 to 90% from the first to the third sampling after application (47 days). Observations from two LSWB of a different study show metazachlor concentrations of 0,764–10.24 \( \mu \)g L\(^{-1}\) (LELF, 2014) considerably higher than those in our study with a maximum of 0,62 \( \mu \)g L\(^{-1}\).

The metazachlor TPs were quantified in maximal concentration of up to 1.8 \( \mu \)g OA L\(^{-1}\) and 4.8 \( \mu \)g ESA L\(^{-1}\). Both TPs show the same patterns just vary in concentration: the concentrations increase overtime to the highest value in the third sample after application in A4, A5, A8. But in A2 and A9, the concentrations were at a constant value and did not change considerably. Metazachlor-ESA concentrations are in general higher than those of metazachlor-OA which can be explained by the ESA's higher occurrence fraction, a higher DT50 in soil and a very low k_foc displaying a very high mobility (PPDB, 2017, Lewis et al., 2016). However, positives in the range of 0.49–4.2 \( \mu \)g L\(^{-1}\) in the samples collected before application cannot be explained. The physicochemical properties, if available, do not predict this persistence. In addition, there was no application of metazachlor in the previous year 2014. This leads to the conclusion that either the TPs are very persistent and are still detectable two years later or transported from former applications at other sites to the LSWB below surface according to the assumptions of Lischeid et al. (2017).

Long-term stability of cladoceran assemblages in small, shallow, Canadian Shield lakes experiencing marked calcium declines L. E. Mosscrop1 · A. M. Paterson2 · A. M. DeSellas2 · J. Kurek3 · R. Weeber4 · J. P. Smol1 Received: 14 May 2014 / Accepted: 2 July 2015 / Published online: 17 July 2015 © Crown Copyright 2015 Abstract A greater appreciation of biotic responses to environmental changes is warranted in small, shallow lakes because of the high number of these habitats, and their unique contributions to regional biodiversity. Furthermore, recent water chemistry monitoring data show that shallow lakes in Ontario are sensitive and have responded significantly to environmental stressors such as acid deposition and lake water calcium decline. Here, we use paleoecological techniques to examine cladoceran assemblages in modern and pre-industrial sediments of 30 shallow lakes to determine the key environmental gradients that influence present-day assemblages, and to assess how assemblage structure has changed since pre-industrial times (pre-1850s). Redundancy analysis of present-day cladoceran assemblages and key environmental variables identified lake surface area and Secchi depth as significant predictors of assemblage composition. In our data set, Secchi depth was not correlated to water clarity but rather to macrophyte cover, suggesting that cladoceran assemblages were highly influenced by habitat structure. In contrast to nearby, deeper lakes, where pelagic cladoceran taxa have changed significantly in relative abundance over time, cladoceran assemblages in present-day and pre-industrial sediments of shallow lakes did not differ significantly in composition. While the specific reasons for this muted response are unknown, we hypothesize that: (1) littoral taxa may be less sensitive to low Ca concentrations, or ecological thresholds have not yet been crossed or are lower for littoral taxa; (2) calcium availability may vary spatially within shallow lakes, and this is not captured in a single measure of water chemistry from the centre of the lake; and/or (3) habitat structure is more important than water chemistry as a predictor of assemblage composition in these study lakes, and this has not changed significantly over time. Keywords Canadian Shield · Calcium · Cladocera · Paleolimnology · Shallow lakes Introduction Long-term declines in calcium (Ca) concentrations have been identified as a significant threat to biological communities in softwater lakes within the Precambrian Shield (Jezierski et al. 2008). In relatively deep lakes, an ominous symptom of this “aquatic osteoporosis” is a decline in the relative abundances of keystone grazers, such as the Ca-sensitive cladoceran Daphnia pulex (Jezierski et al. 2008, 2015), as lake water Ca concentrations near a laboratory-determined threshold of approximately 1.5 mg/L (Ashforth and Yan 2008). These findings were recently confirmed in paleolimnological assessments of softwater, oligotrophic lakes in the Muskoka-Haliburton region of south-central Ontario (DeSellas et al. 2011; Jezierski et al. 2012a, b), where changes in the composition of sedimentary cladoceran assemblages since pre-industrial times were generally consistent with declining calcium concentrations in relatively deep, thermally-stratified lakes. However, it is apparent that shallow and deeper lakes may respond differently to environmental stressors, because of greater interactions at the sediment–water interface, differences in nutrient cycling and availability, and enhanced coupling of the terrestrial environment with the littoral zone in shallow systems (Scheffer 2004), in addition to differing predation regimes (Wellborn et al. 1996). In shallow lakes, the sediment–water interface typically has a higher influence on water quality, aquatic macrophytes and other biota (Tessier and Woodruff 2002; Scheffer 2004), with greater sediment–water contact resulting in increased sediment re-suspension, turbidity, internal nutrient loading, and possibly planktonic productivity. Furthermore, environmental and substrate conditions within the littoral zone are often complex and highly heterogeneous, resulting in diverse assemblages of macro- and micro-flora and fauna. Despite their prevalence across the Boreal Shield, limnological data for shallow lakes in Ontario, Canada, are sparse relative to deeper lakes. Nevertheless, recent monitoring data from softwater, shallow lakes clearly show that they are sensitive, and have responded chemically to environmental stressors such as acid deposition and lake water calcium decline. For example, the shallow lakes of the Muskoka-Haliburton region (referred to as the “Muskoka (CWS)” lakes) have declined by 26 % in lake water calcium concentrations, on average, since monitoring began in the 1980s (Jezierski et al. 2008). What is currently unknown, however, is whether or not these marked chemical changes have altered biological communities over time, as has been reported for deeper, dimictic lakes in the region. Recent work by Shapiera et al. (2011) has shown that some littoral microcrustacean taxa (i.e., Alona rectangula, Disparalona spp., Pleuroxis truncates, and Scapholebris rammneri) have Ca burdens comparable to Ca-rich daphniids, suggesting that some of the inhabitants of the littoral zone may be less competitive at low Ca concentrations. A greater appreciation of biotic responses to environmental changes is warranted in small, shallow lakes because of the high number of these habitats (Minns et al. 2008), and their unique contributions to regional biodiversity. In order to determine the dominant factors influencing cladoceran assemblages in shallow, Canadian Shield lakes, we examine long-term changes in sedimentary cladoceran assemblages in thirty shallow lakes in the Muskoka region of south-central Ontario [a subset of the “Muskoka (CWS)” lakes noted in Jezierski et al. (2008)]. These lakes are relatively undisturbed by local watershed impacts (e.g., shoreline development, forestry operations), but are affected by regional stressors, such as climate change, acidification, and declines in lake water calcium levels. Using paleolimnological techniques, we ask: (1) What are the key environmental gradients that influence sedimentary cladoceran assemblages within these shallow lakes? (2) How does water chemistry and cladoceran assemblage structure in these shallow lakes compare to those recorded by DeSellas et al. (2008, 2011) in nearby, deeper, thermally-stratified lakes? and (3) How has cladoceran assemblage structure changed in these shallow lakes since pre-industrial times (pre-1850s)? Given the significant changes in water chemistry that have been observed in these shallow lakes over the past few decades (particularly long-term declines in lake Ca concentrations), we expect cladoceran assemblage structure to respond accordingly, as has been observed in nearby, deeper lakes (e.g., Jezierski et al. 2008). Specifically, we anticipate that the relative abundance of littoral taxa requiring higher levels of Ca will be lower in modern lake sediments. Materials and methods Study area and field sampling The thirty study lakes are located within relatively remote, boreal forests of the Canadian Shield in the Muskoka-Haliburton region of south-central Ontario (Fig. 1; Table 1). The lakes were chosen from a subset of lakes sampled by the Canadian Wildlife Service (CWS) as part of Environment Canada’s Acid Rain program, a biological monitoring program designed to assess the impacts of acidifying deposition on wildlife and their habitats in eastern Canada (McNicol et al. 1996). Lakes were selected for study from the CWS lake set if they were less than 7 m in maximum depth, and within 3 km of an accessible road. The region lies at the southern limit of the Boreal Ecozone, and forest composition ranges from predominantly coniferous to mixed hardwood. Conifer, mixed, and thicket swamps are the dominant peatland types. The lakes and watersheds are underlain by Precambrian granitic bedrock (Jeffries and Snyder 1983). The shallow and acidic soils are low in nutrients, with local deposits of clay, sand and gravel apparent in some of the watersheds (Chapman and Putnam 1984). Regional stressors affecting lakes in the area are derived, in part, from seasonal cottages, recreational activities associated with cottages, and infrastructure required by populations from organized towns and hamlets. However, the majority of the shallow lakes (27 of 30) included in this study do not have residences located within their local catchments. This area has an active forestry industry and it is likely that the majority of the catchments have been logged in the past, and several have active, selective tree-cutting programs that may have contributed to recent declines in lake water Ca concentrations (Watmough et al. 2003). Fig. 1 Map showing the location of the 30 study lakes in south-central Ontario, Canada Water chemistry was collected on a regular basis between 1990 and 2009 by CWS, except for Heney Lake, which has been sampled by the Ontario Ministry of the Environment’s Dorset Environmental Science Centre (DESC; www.desc.ca) since 1979. Available water chemistry data include nutrients [total phosphorus (TP), Total Kjeldahl Nitrogen (TKN), nitrate + nitrite (NO_3/NO_2), ammonia (NH_3)], dissolved inorganic carbon (DIC), dissolved organic carbon (DOC), major cations and anions [calcium (Ca), potassium (K), sodium (Na), magnesium (Mg), sulphate (SO_4), conductivity (cond)], and measures of acidity [pH, Gran alkalinity (Alk)]. TN was calculated as the mass sum of TKN and NO_3/NO_2. Maximum lake depth (Zmax) was measured on site and lake area (ha) was provided by CWS. Secchi depth (cm), surface water temperature, and an estimate of relative macrophyte cover (%; available for 25 of the study lakes) were measured at the time of core collection (July 25 to August 12, 2011). Importantly, Secchi depth estimates were not a direct measure of water clarity in six of the study lakes, where the disc was obscured by dense macrophyte growth (lakes 1204, 1215, 1230, 1331, 1336, 1511). Relative macrophyte coverage (%) was assessed by dividing each lake into sections, estimating % macrophyte coverage within sections, and then averaging these estimates to produce a single, lakewide estimate. Glew (1989) sediment cores were sampled at the deepest point of each of the 30 study lakes in the summer of 2011. The cores were extruded on shore using a Glew (1988) vertical extruder and the top and bottom 2-cm of sediment was sectioned at 0.25-cm intervals. Bottom sediments were not collected from four of the lakes because core lengths were less than 4 cm. Bottom sediments were considered only if the core was longer than 15 cm, as previous dating of sediment cores from lakes in this region has reported the background time period (i.e., pre-1850) to fall between core depths of \( \sim 15 \) and 20 cm (Mills et al. 2009; Moss-crop 2013). Laboratory analyses Replicate microscope slides from the top and bottom samples from each of the 30 lakes were prepared for cladoceran analyses following techniques outlined in Korhola and Rautio (2001). Sediment was deflocculated in a 10 % KOH solution and heated at 80 °C for approximately 30 min. The sediment was then passed through a 37-μm sieve and rinsed with de-ionized water. The residue that was retained on the sieve was transferred to a small vial using de-ionized water. Two to three drops of ethanol were added to prevent fungal growth, and two to three drops of safranin-glycerin solution were added to stain the cladoceran remains. Finally, samples were mixed and 50-μl aliquots were pipetted on to slides, and permanent slides were made using glycerin jelly. Taxonomic identifications of fossil cladocerans followed Szeroczynska and Sarmaja-Korjonen (2007) and Korosi and Smol (2012a, b). Cladoceran remains were identified under 20× or 40× magnification (10× ocular lens) using a Leica DMRB light microscope with bright field optics. Slides were scanned in their entirety to ensure that all identifiable remains were counted. All cladoceran remains (e.g., carapaces, headshields and post-abdominal claws) were tabulated separately for each taxon. The most abundant remain was then used to calculate the number of individuals (Frey 1986). Usually 2–5 slides were sufficient to enumerate 100 individual cladocerans; however, five of the 30 lakes had low cladoceran counts (i.e., under 100 individuals), although above the recommended minimum of 70 individuals (Kurek et al. 2010a). Daphnia were separated into two groups based on postabdominal claw morphology [i.e., D. pulex complex (stout middle pectin) or D. longispina complex (uniform middle pectin); Korosi et al. (2011)]. Bosminids were not separated into individual species (i.e., Eubosmina and Bosmina longirostris) but were grouped as Bosmina spp. Statistical analyses Shallow lake set Principal components analysis (PCA: correlation matrix) was used to examine the variation in present-day water chemistry across lakes. Prior to statistical analyses, site 1503 was identified as an outlier, both chemically (>95 % CI of PCA Axis 1 scores of environmental data) and biologically (>90 % CI of PCA Axis 1 scores of cladoceran assemblage data), and thus removed from subsequent tests of the modern data. The shallow lakes of the Muskoka-Haliburton region were last sampled by CWS for water chemistry in the autumns of 2007, 2008 or 2009 using a bottle grab sample from the surface waters. Although coring occurred in 2011, the 2007-09 water chemistry data were considered to be representative of present-day conditions, as water chemistry in regional lakes (Zmax: 5.8–38 m) has changed little over the past 3-5 years relative to changes that have occurred over the past three decades (Palmer et al. 2011). Environmental variables, with the exception of Alk, Secchi, pH, Mg, K, NO3/NO2, TN were either log (area, Zmax, cond, TP, NH3, SO4), square root (DIC) or ln (x + 1) (Ca, DOC) transformed, where x was the environmental variable under consideration, to stabilize variances in the data. Prior to statistical analyses, the cladoceran data were pre-screened for rare taxa. Cladoceran taxa that did not occur in at least two lakes with a relative abundance of at least 2 % were removed from further statistical analyses. Detrended correspondence analysis (DCA) on square-root transformed species data, with detrending by segments, was used to determine the amount of taxa turnover. Because of the short gradient lengths of the first DCA axis of species data (i.e. <2 SD units), linear ordination techniques (PCA and Redundancy Analysis, RDA) were used to: (1) examine the variation in present-day cladoceran assemblages across lakes; and (2) explore the relationships between cladoceran species and environmental data, and to select the minimum set of environmental variables that best described the distribution of species (ter Braak and Šmilauer 2002). For RDA, manual forward selection was used to determine significant (p < 0.05) environmental predictors. Assemblage similarities were calculated using the Bray-Curtis similarity coefficient (Bray and Curtis 1957) on square-root transformed species data, and used to construct a similarity matrix among modern (present-day) and pre-industrial sediment samples. Using this matrix, a one-way analysis of similarities (ANOSIM) was calculated to test for significant differences in cladoceran assemblage composition between modern and pre-industrial sediment samples using the Paleontological Statistics (PAST) program (v2.16; Hammer et al. 2001). Following ANOSIM, dominant cladoceran taxonomic groups (Bosmina spp, Chydoridae, Daphnia, Holopedium glacialis, and Macrothricidae) in pre-industrial (bottom) and modern (top) sediments were compared individually using a Wilcoxon Signed-Rank test with corrected p-values. Comparing water chemistry and cladoceran assemblages in the 30 shallow and 41 deeper lakes DeSellas et al. (2008, 2011) studied current conditions and long-term changes in cladoceran assemblages in deeper and generally larger lakes within Muskoka-Haliburton. Because the cladocerans were processed and identified in the same lab using similar techniques, it was possible to compare water chemistry and cladoceran assemblage structure in the surface sediments of the shallow and deeper lakes. Prior to comparison, the following adjustments were made to ensure taxonomic harmonization of Cladocera in the datasets: (1) Eubosmina and Bosmina were combined, because this taxonomic differentiation was not made in the shallow lake set; (2) Daphniids were combined into D. pulex (stout pecten) and D. longispina (uniform, fine pecten) complexes; (3) Sididae were combined; and (4) Macrothricidae were combined. Water chemistry was also simplified in the comparison of shallow and deeper lakes, as there were differences in the variables analysed. We included nutrients (TP, NO3/NO2), DIC, DOC, major cations and anions (Ca, K, Na, Mg, SO4, cond), pH, and lake morphometric variables (Zmax and lake surface area). Untransformed water chemistry variables from the shallow (n = 30) and deep (n = 41) lakes were compared in SigmaStat v3.1 using Mann–Whitney Rank Sum tests. For ordination analyses, environmental variables, with the exception of pH, Mg, K, NO3/NO2, were either log (x + 1) (area, Zmax, cond, TP, SO4), square-root (DIC) or ln (x + 1) (Ca, DOC) transformed, where x was the environmental variable under consideration. RDA with manual forward selection was run on the combined dataset (including both shallow and deeper lakes) to explore the relationship between cladoceran taxa and environmental data across the broader predictor gradients. Cladoceran assemblages in the present-day sediments of shallow and deeper lakes were also compared using ANOSIM, and the cladoceran taxa responsible for the observed differences in assemblage composition between the lake sets were identified using the statistical procedure Similarity Percentages (SIMPER; Clarke 1993). Results and discussion Lakes in the Muskoka-Haliburton region of south-central Ontario have recorded significant changes in water chemistry over the past few decades, including increases in DOC, declines in Ca concentrations, and declines in TP concentrations (Mallory et al. 1998; Jeziorski et al. 2008; Palmer et al. 2011). For some measures (e.g., Ca), the chemical changes observed in shallow lakes were larger than those recorded in nearby, deeper lakes (Jeziorski et al. 2008). However, despite changes in water chemistry over the past few decades, and significant changes in cladoceran assemblages observed in neighbouring, deeper lakes in south-central Ontario since pre-industrial times (DeSellas et al. 2011), we observed minimal change in cladoceran assemblages in a comparison of modern and pre-industrial sediments of thirty small, shallow lakes. Beginning with an exploration of present-day water chemistry and its relationship to modern cladoceran assemblages, we discuss our findings below, focussing first on the shallow lake dataset, and then combining these data with previously published cladoceran analyses from nearby, deeper lakes. Water chemistry in shallow lakes The first (\( \lambda = 0.36 \)) and second (\( \lambda = 0.21 \)) PCA axes captured 57 % of the variation in the water chemistry data from shallow lakes (Fig. 2). The first axis showed strong positive correlations with pH, Alk, Ca, Mg, specific conductance, and DIC. The second PCA axis was strongly positively correlated with lake surface area (ha), Secchi depth, and SO\(_4\), and showed weaker negative correlations with TP, TN and DOC. As reported in surveys from deeper lakes (Paterson et al. 2001; DeSellas et al. 2008), the first axis likely reflects natural variation in surficial geology, from more acidic sites with shallow soils to sites with thicker deposits of till. This, in turn, regulates the sensitivity of sites to acidic deposition, with PCA axis 1 separating dilute lakes with low buffering capacities (i.e., bottom left quadrant) from lakes with relatively higher ionic concentrations (Fig. 2). As reported in other regional surveys (e.g., Paterson et al. 2001; Kurek et al. 2010b), lake area was negatively correlated with nutrient (TN, TP) and DOC concentrations. In part, this may be related to differences in drainage ratios and lake volumes, with smaller, more productive lakes in the dataset receiving higher areal inputs of nutrients and DOC. Small, shallow lakes also have lower ratios of lake volume/sediment surface area, and thus may experience higher relative inputs of nutrients from lake sediments, particularly during periods of higher productivity (i.e., during the ice-free season) (Søndergaard et al. 2003), or during periods of higher water column stability. Cladocera in the surface sediments of shallow lakes and their relationship to environmental variables In general, fossil cladocerans from both the surface (30 lakes) and pre-industrial (26 lakes) sediments of the shallow study lakes were well preserved and abundant, with the samples dominated by taxa of the families Bosminidae and Chydoridae. However, the uppermost 0–0.25 cm sediment interval had very few remains in most lakes (i.e., the top intervals were sampled conservatively in order to preserve the sediment–water interface, and contained little sediment after freeze drying), and therefore the 0.25–0.5 cm interval was used to represent modern conditions. Forty-five cladoceran taxa were identified in the surface sediments of the 30 shallow lakes, with 25 remaining for statistical analyses after removing rare taxa (Table 2). Bosmina spp. was the dominant taxon in the majority of the lakes, with a mean relative abundance of 42.7 %, and with relative abundances of more than 50 % in 16 of 30 lakes. However, four lakes (1204, 1503, 1506, 1537) had less than 10 % abundance of Bosmina spp., which tends to be a rare occurrence in larger, deeper lakes (DeSellas et al. 2008; Kurek et al. 2010b). Forward selection in RDA identified two environmental variables (Secchi depth and lake surface area) that explained significant (p = 0.005) amounts of variation in the cladoceran data (Fig. 3). When constrained to these variables, the first two RDA axes explained 20 % of the variation in the cladoceran species data, although most of the explained variation was loaded onto RDA Axis 1. In the shallow lake dataset, with the exception of a weak relationship with NO3/NO2, Secchi depth was not significantly correlated to any other water chemistry variable, despite showing strong correlations with DOC, colour, and nutrient concentrations in deeper lakes (e.g., Pérez-Fuentetaja et al. 1999). This may be because Secchi depth measurements were obscured by dense macrophyte beds in six lakes, and so was not a true measure of water clarity across the lakes. Thus, as reported in other studies of shallow lakes (e.g., Chambers and Kalff 1985; Cheruvelil and Soranno 2008), Secchi depth serves as a reasonable surrogate for percent macrophyte coverage in our dataset (Fig. 4a), reflecting differences in habitat structure among lakes. Many littoral and benthic Cladocera are influenced by macrophyte density (Tremel et al. 2000; Yarwood-Buchanan 2005; Declerck et al. 2011), and our results confirm that habitat structure is an important predictor of sedimentary cladoceran composition in shallow lakes (<7 m) in south-central Ontario. For example, Bosmina spp. were found generally at higher relative abundances in larger lakes with fewer macrophytes, whereas members of the Fig. 4 Scatterplots showing the relationship between: a percent macrophyte cover and Secchi depth; and PCA Axis 1 scores of sedimentary cladoceran remains and Secchi depth (b), for shallow lakes in south-central Ontario, Canada Chydoridae were more prevalent in the smaller, macrophyte-rich lakes (Fig. 3). A comparison of the main direction of variation in the modern cladoceran assemblage (PCA Axis 1 sample scores of the species data) with Secchi depth showed a significant linear relationship, suggesting that Secchi depth, and thus macrophyte cover (Fig. 4a), tracked an important direction of variation in the fossil cladoceran data (Fig. 4b). It is worth noting that our results differ from a recent survey of littoral microcrustacean assemblages from 22 Canadian Shield lakes in south-central Ontario. Walseng et al. (2008) examined the relative importance of acidity and habitat structure as regulators of littoral microcrustacean assemblage composition, as previous studies had reported the importance of both as predictors (e.g., acidity: Walseng et al. 2001; Hann and Turner 2000; e.g., habitat structure: Tremel et al. 2000). In their survey, Walseng et al. (2008) found little difference in assemblage composition in wave-washed sandy habitats versus more protected habitats dominated by floating-leaved macrophytes. Furthermore, lake water pH was found to be strongly correlated with the main direction of variation in the species data (Walseng et al. 2008). The apparent discrepancy in the above studies and our results likely stems from the much narrower chemical gradient examined in our study lakes (e.g., our study, pH 5.4–6.1; Walseng et al. 2008, pH 4.6–6.9), and our more general definition of habitat structure (low to high macrophyte cover). As described below (‘Comparing water chemistry and Cladocera in shallow and deeper lakes’), we found that water chemistry increased in importance as a predictor of cladoceran assemblage composition when the chemical gradient was broadened, as was the case when we combined our shallow lake data with those from 41 deeper lakes. Similarly, in a survey of cladoceran assemblages from the surface sediments of 50 moderately deep (mean Zmax = 10.6 m) Boreal Shield lakes in northwestern Ontario, water chemistry and lake surface area explained the largest amount of unique variation in the data set (Kurek et al. 2011). Cladoceran assemblages in top–bottom paleolimnological assessments of shallow lakes The cladoceran assemblages recorded in the modern and pre-industrial sediment samples were not significantly different (Fig. 5; ANOSIM, R = 0.01, p = 0.22, n = 26), with Bosmina spp. the dominant taxon in both time periods. Univariate analyses of the dominant taxa showed that only the Macrothricidae, which in these lakes included Acantholeberis curvirostris and Ophryoxus gracilis, were significantly different (i.e., lower in relative abundance in the modern samples) in modern and pre-industrial sediments (p < 0.05). Members of this family are generally considered to be tolerant of lower ionic concentrations and more acidic conditions (Fryer 1980; Walseng et al. 2003) and, as scraper feeders, commonly live in close association with macrophytes (Elmoor-Loureiro 2007). However, these are conditions that describe many of the lakes currently, and so the decrease in Macrothricidae over time cannot easily be explained by these general ecological characteristics. The other most common cladoceran groups, including littoral taxa, did not change significantly from pre-industrial to modern times (p > 0.05), when examined across all lakes. In contrast to nearby, deeper lakes, where significant changes in cladoceran assemblages have been observed since pre-industrial times (DeSellas et al. 2011), species composition in shallow lakes was remarkably stable in a comparison of present-day and pre-industrial sediments. In the deeper lakes, changes were linked to the interactive effects of several environmental stressors, resulting in long-term changes in water chemistry. Similarly, Shapiera et al. (2011) demonstrated that several littoral microcrustacean taxa differ in their Ca content, as shown for Daphnia spp. (Jeziorski and Yan 2006), suggesting littoral cladoceran composition may be sensitive to changes in Ca levels. However, the lack of change in littoral taxa, despite low lake water Ca concentrations and evidence of declining Ca over time, may indicate that: (1) littoral taxa are less sensitive to low Ca concentrations, or ecological thresholds have not yet been crossed, or are lower for littoral taxa; (2) calcium availability varies spatially within shallow lakes, and this is not captured in a single measure of water chemistry from the centre of the lake; and/or (3) habitat structure is more important than water chemistry as a predictor of assemblage composition in these study lakes, and this has not changed significantly over time. The observed differences in the biological response in shallow and deep lakes may also be influenced by other factors, such as a differential response of lakes of varying depths to climatic change. For example, dimictic lakes in south-central Ontario have increased in thermal stability since the 1980s (Palmer et al. 2014), and mixing depths have become shallower because of climate-driven increases in dissolved organic carbon concentrations (Keller 2007). Daphniids, in particular, have been shown to be sensitive to increases in lake water temperatures, and an increased growing season with warming may provide some taxa with an advantage over macroinvertebrate predators, such as Chaoborus (Neill 1981). However, in a recent assessment of long-term trends in zooplankton in Dorset, Ontario lakes (Yan et al. 2008), changes in mean cladoceran body size (the strongest trend) were unrelated to changes in climate indices, and Sweetman et al. (2008) reported no consistent change in planktonic cladoceran communities (bosminids and daphniids) in a top–bottom paleolimnological study of 50 lakes from central Canada, a region that has warmed considerably over the last century. Comparing water chemistry and Cladocera in shallow and deeper lakes Despite similarities in trends over time (e.g., for Ca, Jeziorski et al. 2008), a comparison of modern water chemistry from shallow and nearby, deeper lakes (DeSellas et al. 2008) revealed many significant differences (Fig. 6, Table 3). In general, shallow lakes are smaller, of lower ionic content, and higher in DOC concentrations. The shallow and deeper lakes did not differ significantly in TP concentrations, but NO3/NO2 concentrations were significantly lower in the shallow lakes at the time of sampling (October). Presumably, this was due to its rapid uptake by phytoplankton and periphytic algal communities at the end of the growing season, and because of higher denitrification rates in the more productive shallow lake systems (Søndergaard et al. 2005). Of interest to our study were differences in Ca concentrations, which were significantly lower in the shallow lakes (Fig. 6; Table 3). Although the specific reasons for this difference need to be explored further, lake water Ca concentrations reflect a balance of inputs and losses, with the primary input coming from exchangeable soil sites within the watershed (Houle et al. 2006). It is likely that the smaller, shallow lakes also have smaller catchment areas that are less likely to contain deeper soils, resulting in lower areal export of Ca to surface waters. Furthermore, selective tree-cutting programs in these catchments may have further lowered Ca concentrations through the removal of this Ca pool from the watershed, and its accelerated uptake during forest regrowth (Watmough et al. 2003). Finally, the uptake of calcium by macrophytes in the shallow lakes may also contribute to lower ambient Ca levels, particularly at the end of the growing season, prior to senescence. The combined data set of shallow and deep lakes extended the gradients of all physical and water chemistry variables. As a result, RDA identified lake surface area, maximum depth, Ca, Mg, and SO4 as variables explaining the main direction of variation in the cladoceran assemblage data (Fig. 7). RDA Axis 1 clearly separated the small, shallow lakes from the larger, deeper lakes examined by DeSellas et al. (2008). A closer examination of the data showed that certain pelagic taxa, such as Daphnia (both the D. pulex and D. longispina complexes), were rarely found in the shallow lakes (on average only 2 % relative abundance). Larger Daphnia species, for example, may experience reduced predation pressure in deeper lakes with vertical diel migration (Jeppesen et al. 1997). Three pelagic taxa (Bosmina spp., D. pulex complex and Daphnia longispina complex) contributed to more than half of the dissimilarity (Table 4), occurring in higher relative abundances in the deeper lakes, again reflecting the clear separation of assemblages based on lake depth and corresponding habitat dominance of either the pelagic or littoral zone (Fig. 8). Conclusions In an examination of cladoceran assemblages in present-day and pre-industrial sediments from thirty shallow lakes in south-central Ontario, we found modern cladoceran assemblages to be highly influenced by habitat structure. Secchi depth (related to macrophyte cover) and lake area were shown to be important predictors of assemblage composition in lakes <7 m in depth. A top–bottom paleolimnological analyses revealed that cladoceran assemblage structure was relatively stable through time in the shallow lakes, despite significant changes in our water chemistry data over the last few decades. These results suggest that littoral Cladocera are less influenced by changes in water chemistry than pelagic taxa, including significant declines in Ca concentrations, a surprising result given the variation that exists among littoral taxa in Ca content (Shapiera et al. 2011), and evidence of significant biological change having occurred in nearby, deeper lakes. Further analyses on continuous sedimentary records are recommended to confirm these patterns through time, and to obtain additional information on changes in water quality and biological condition in shallow lakes in the region. These analyses should include an examination of other palaeoecological indicators (e.g., diatoms; sedimentary chlorophyll \( a \)) to reconstruct long-term changes in water quality and ecological condition. Laboratory analyses Replicate microscope slides from the top and bottom samples from each of the 30 lakes were prepared for cladoceran analyses following techniques outlined in Korhola and Rautio (2001). Sediment was deflocculated in a 10 % KOH solution and heated at 80 °C for approximately 30 min. The sediment was then passed through a 37-μm sieve and rinsed with de-ionized water. The residue that was retained on the sieve was transferred to a small vial using de-ionized water. Two to three drops of ethanol were added to prevent fungal growth, and two to three drops of safranin-glycerin solution were added to stain the cladoceran remains. Finally, samples were mixed and 50-μl aliquots were pipetted on to slides, and permanent slides were made using glycerin jelly. Taxonomic identifications of fossil cladocerans followed Szeroczynska and Sarmaja-Korjonen (2007) and Korosi and Smol (2012a, b). Cladoceran remains were identified under 20× or 40× magnification (10× ocular lens) using a Leica DMRB light microscope with bright field optics. Slides were scanned in their entirety to ensure that all identifiable remains were counted. All cladoceran remains (e.g., carapaces, headshields and post-abdominal claws) were tabulated separately for each taxon. The most abundant remain was then used to calculate the number of individuals (Frey 1986). Usually 2–5 slides were sufficient to enumerate 100 individual cladocerans; however, five of the 30 lakes had low cladoceran counts (i.e., under 100 individuals), although above the recommended minimum of 70 individuals (Kurek et al. 2010a). Daphnia were separated into two groups based on postabdominal claw morphology [i.e., D. pulex complex (stout middle pectin) or D. longispina complex (uniform middle pectin); Korosi et al. (2011)]. Bosminids were not separated into individual species (i.e., Eubosmina and Bosmina longirostris) but were grouped as Bosmina spp.

Monitoring status, habitat features and amphibian species richness of Crested newt (Triturus cristatus superspecies) ponds at the edge of the species range (Salzburg, Austria) A. Maletzky1*, M. Kyek2, A. Goldschmid1 1 University of Salzburg, Department of Organismic Biology, Hellbrunnerstrasse 34, A-5020 Salzburg. 2 Institute of Ecology, Johann Herbst Strasse 23, A-5061 Elsbethen. We studied the status of Crested newt (Triturus cristatus superspecies) ponds in the province of Salzburg during the years 2004 and 2005. Historical and current distribution data were collected and compared. In the end of 2004, 51 ponds with Crested newt records of which 39 still existed were known in Salzburg. In 2005 we carried out a monitoring of these ponds using a combination of three survey methods. Presence or absence of adult and larval Crested newts and the number of syntopic amphibian species were recorded. Detection probabilities and the effects of seven characteristic pond features on pond occupancy were calculated for adult and larval newts separately. We observed a strong decline of ponds occupied by Crested newts with presence of adults in 22 and presence of larvae in 16 surveyed ponds, respectively. Detection probabilities imply that we detected all ponds occupied by adults and larvae. Key habitat features for Crested newt presence are low degree of shading for adults and larvae as well as a high density of submerged vegetation for larvae. Pond size and depth are not significant. Furthermore we recorded a significantly higher number of amphibian species in ponds occupied by Crested newts. Our results might aid in the implementation of sustainable measures for a conservation of these critically endangered species in the province of Salzburg. Keywords: Habitat features, monitoring, pond occupancy, Salzburg, Triturus cristatus superspecies. Introduction During the past decades a decline of amphibian populations in many parts of the world has been observed (e.g. Wake 1991, Houlahan et al. 2000). There are several hypotheses to account for this decline on the global scale. Most probably a combination of many factors is responsible (Collins & Storfer 2003). In the case of the highly urbanised and developed countries of Central and Western Europe, the major factor is without doubt the loss of natural and functioning pond networks (Oertli et al. 2005), due to destruction and manipulation of wetlands and ponds (e.g. Corbett 1989, Beebee 1997, Wood et al. 2003). The province of Salzburg (Austria) consists of a variety of habitats within a vertical range of 380 to 3600 m above sea level. Hence there exists a great variety of pond types facing many different threats. Especially in the lowland areas of the North and the inner alpine river valleys, the number of ponds in natural conditions has decreased throughout the past decades due to intensive anthropogenic pressure and land use. Most of the remaining ponds are artificial and often densely stocked with fish and waterfowl (Kyek & Maletzky 2006). At present the occurrence of 15 amphibian species is documented, of which 13 are reproducing in standing water bodies. Four species have been classified as critically endangered in the current regional Red List of amphibians and reptiles, including the two occurring Crested newt species (Triturus cristatus, Laurenti 1768 and Triturus carnifex, Laurenti 1768) (Kyek & Maletzky 2006). Crested newts (Triturus cristatus superspecies) are distributed over great parts of Europe with populations showing significant declines in large parts of this area (Gasc et al. 1997). As these species are listed in Annex II and IV of the EU-habitats directive 92/43/EEC as well as Annex II of the Bern Convention, their conservation status is of European importance. The populations in the province of Salzburg are of special interest, being located in a part of their distribution areas, where the two species can be found narrowly sympatric and hybrid populations exist (e.g. Freytag, 1978, Thiesmeier & Kupfer 2000, Arntzen 2003). For this study we therefore stick to the taxon Triturus cristatus superspecies. The results of a survey on the identification of the species using molecular methods are in preparation (Maletzky unpublished data). Due to their wide distribution area Crested newts inhabit a variety of pond types. Generally these water bodies can be described as large and deep with submerged vegetation and absence of fish (Arntzen 2003). The characteristics of suitable ponds depend more on the particular landscape features than on the particular species (e.g. Cabela & Grillitsch 2001, Arntzen 2003). The quality and quantity of these characteristics in part determines the presence and size of the populations (Oldham et al. 2000). Monitoring the distribution and the key habitat features is among the most important requirements for the effective conservation management of threatened species at regional level. A major problem with most monitoring programs is that species are detected imperfectly, which might lead to biased estimates of population trends (MacKenzie et al. 2002, Schmidt 2005). A determination of key habitat features can serve as a basis for detecting the likelihood of occurrence and a guideline for habitat enhancement and creation. Already several studies dealt with the selection and suitability of amphibian breeding habitats using multivariate analysis (Pavignano et al. 1990), discriminant analysis (Swan & Oldham 1994) or logistic regression (Laurila 1998). Key habitat criteria for Crested newt species have been evaluated mainly in core distribution areas of T. carnifex (Pavignano et al. 1990) and of T. cristatus (Oldham et al. 2000). The aims of this study are (1) to evaluate the status of Crested newts in the province of Salzburg, (2) to identify key habitat features for their occurrence in ponds, and (3) to develop standards for the creation or enhancement of ponds supporting these critically endangered species at the edge of their distribution range. Materials and methods Study area The study area covers the three northern districts of the province of Salzburg ("Salzburg Stadt", "Salzburg Land", "Hallein"), with a total area of 1777 km². The main landscape features are the valley of the lower Salzach River, parts of the northern Limestone Alps, Flysch zone and the foothills of the Alps with the lake district (Fig. 1). Historical data Although there are some historical records on the occurrence of Crested newts in Salzburg (e.g. Woltersstorff 1925, Schüller 1963, Freytag 1978), data on precise localities and structure of ponds are scarce. Some information could be drawn from unpublished mapping projects (Kyek unpublished data) and the collection of L. Schüller located in the Natural History Museum "Haus der Natur", Salzburg. Geographical coordinates (± 100-500 m) and habitat descriptions of the origin of preserved specimens were attributed to each record as precise as possible. Together with more recent records collected by the authors, Crested newts were known from 44 ponds between the years 1949 and 2003. Monitoring We examined the status of the 44 ponds with previous records of Crested newts in 2004 and carried out a monitoring of the ponds that were still existing as well as new found localities in 2005. Presence or absence of Crested newt adults and larvae as well as syntopic amphibian species was recorded during three visits per pond between April and July. We used a combination of detection methods with bottle traps, night ![Geographical distribution of monitored Crested newt (Triturus cristatus superspecies) ponds in 2005. Solid triangle = unconfirmed localities (n = 16); Encircled solid triangles = confirmed localities (n = 22).](page_1092_320_1012_1012.png) Fig. 1 Geographical distribution of monitored Crested newt (Triturus cristatus superspecies) ponds in 2005. Solid triangle = unconfirmed localities (n = 16); Encircled solid triangles = confirmed localities (n = 22). counting and dip-netting. Bottle traps were the main tool for detection and used in each of the three surveys. Such traps are especially useful for presence-absence surveys in ponds that are big or otherwise difficult to examine (Griffiths 1985). We used a minimum number of 10 traps per pond and placed one trap at least every 5 meters. Traps were positioned mainly in shallow water areas with an angle of about 45°. A small perforated part remaining above the water surface allowed the captured individuals to breathe (H. Schedl, pers. comm.). The traps were active overnight from late afternoon to the following morning. The second visit was accompanied by additional night counting, while the third visit was especially focussed on the detection of larvae by means of dip-netting. Habitat features We recorded the particular pond type using the standardized mapping form for monitoring the Austrian herpetofauna (Kyek 1996). Furthermore we recorded 7 habitat features for Crested newt ponds including pond area (m²), maximum depth in three classes (<30 cm, 30-100 cm, >100 cm), fish presence or absence, origin (natural or artificial), and presence or absence of human use. We also estimated density of submerged vegetation (in 25 %-classes) and proportion of shade (in 25 %-classes). Data analysis All mapping and monitoring data were processed with BioOffice-databanking (©Biogis) and ArcView 9.1 for GIS (© Esri). For the monitoring data of the year 2005 we estimated detection probabilities and the proportion of sites occupied by adults and larvae separately, using the mark recapture like approach of MacKenzie et al. (2002, 2005). The analysis was done with the software Presence 2.0. The effects of habitat variables on the presence of Crested newts, adults and larvae, were analysed by means of logistic regression, which was performed with R freeware (R Development Core Team 2005). We used the Firth's bias reduced logistic regression implemented in the LOGISTF-package (Ploner et al. 2006). Results Status and monitoring of Crested newt ponds While 32 (72.7 %) ponds with old records still exist, all ponds with records before 1977 have been destroyed. In contrast, we recorded Crested newt presence in 7 ponds which were evaluated for the first time in the two study years. Therefore to date, 39 (out of a total of 51 records) Crested newt ponds are known in the province of Salzburg. One private garden pond could not be surveyed in the course of this study. During the monitoring of 38 ponds in 2005 the presence of adult Crested newts was recorded for 22 ponds (57.9 %), larvae were detected in 16 ponds (42.1 %) (Fig. 1, Tab. 1), while 16 ponds were classified as unoccupied Crested newt ponds (Tab. 2). We analysed detection probabilities for adults and larvae separately. Therefore we first tested two pre-defined models that used constant and survey-specific detection probabilities. For both adults and larvae the lower AIC value indicated that the survey-specific P model was better supported by the data and detection probabilities were time specific. The predicted site occupancy using this model was 0.588 (SE = 0.082) for adults and 0.431 (SE = 0.081) for larvae, respectively (Tab. 3). While detection probabilities (P) for adults were high in all three surveys ranging from 0.640 to 0.951, detection probabilities for larvae were very low in the first two surveys but high (i.e. P = 1.000) in the third one (Tab. 4). These results imply that we detected all the ponds where adult and larval Crested newts were present. Habitat features of studied ponds The mean water surface area of studied ponds (n = 38) was 342.2 m² (± 425.2 m² std. dev.) with a range of 20-2000 m². The majority of ponds showed maximum depths of 30-100 cm (56.4 %), while a maximum depth of more than 1 meter was recorded for 16 ponds (41.0 %). Only one pond had a maximum depth of less than 30 cm. Fish presence was recorded for 8 (21.1 %) ponds, three of them being densely stocked. Artificial ponds (71.1 %) were built for purposes like fish breeding, ice stock sliding in winter and fire protection. One brewery ice pond that was created to have a cheap possibility of cooling is now used extensively for fish breeding. Private garden ponds are used for swimming or ornamental reasons. Eight ponds (20.5 %) were created in the course of nature conservation projects since 1991. The habitat feature human use contains 25 (65.8 %) of these ponds that are periodically managed and succession is interrupted, which is beneficial for amphibian populations. Thirteen ponds (34.2 %) are not used currently and thus subject to strong succession. The proportion of average area covered by submerged vegetation was 0-25 % in 17 ponds, 26-50 % in 11 and 51-75 % in 9 ponds respectively. Only one pond had 75-100 % submerged vegetation cover. We found that a low degree of shade is the most important habitat variable with significant results in both adult (P > 0.001) and larval (P > 0.05) presence. The latter was also significantly correlated to a high density of submerged vegetation (P > 0.001), which showed a comparably high but not significant probability in adults. The same is true for the variables human use and pond origin. Pond area, maximum depth and fish presence had no significant effects in both cases. Species richness Regression analyses show a highly significant correlation between presence of Crested newt adults and larvae and the number of co-occurring species (P > 0,001; Tab. 5). Altogether 8 further amphibian taxa could be detected in the surveyed ponds. Of these, Alpine newt (Mesotriton alpestris Laurenti, 1768) and Smooth newt (Lissotriton vulgaris L., 1758) were most frequently found in occupied Crested newt ponds (90.9 % each), while they were present in 50 % and 37.5 % of the unoccupied ponds, respectively. The Tree frog (Hyla arborea L., 1758) was detected in 59.1 % of occupied ponds, while there are no records for unoccupied ones. Likewise the Yellow bellied toad (Bombina variegata L., 1758) was only found in occupied ponds with a frequency of 31.8 %. Discussion Status and monitoring of Crested newt ponds The occurrence and frequency of Crested newts (Triturus cristatus superspecies) has declined seriously during the last century. One of the main factors for this pattern is the loss or manipulation of suitable breeding habitats (Arntzen 2003). Our study represents the first approach of a species specific monitoring of amphibian breeding ponds in the province of Salzburg. It shows that about 25 % of all recorded ponds with crested newt presence have disappeared and reproduction was observed in less than 50 % of the existing ponds. Europe have been published throughout the previous decades. In the German federal state of Rhineland-Palatinate the loss of habitats was regarded as 20 % (Bitz & Simon 1996). In Great Britain regional estimates vary widely from 90 % for parts of London to 6 % for urban ponds in Edinburgh (Wood et al. 2003). Monitoring projects of Crested newt populations in neighbouring regions showed comparably low occupation levels. In South-Eastern Bavaria 9 out of 20 surveyed ponds were found unoccupied (Gruber, H.-J. unpublished data). In the province of Lower Austria, Klepsch (1994) found Crested newt presence in only 5 out of 14 sites that were occupied ten years before. These data are similar to the decrease of 1.4 – 2.0 % in population numbers per annum which was estimated for Great Britain (Clemons 1997). The reasons for the declining number of Crested newt populations and habitats in our area are generally related to the fact that these species are restricted to the lowlands and hills in the northern districts. Their distribution area is nearly identical with the main human settlement area, which is underlying increasing pressure from infrastructure and land use. Data on current and historical vertical distribution show that most populations have been lost in the lowlands (Maletzky unpublished data). Species detection in monitoring studies tends to be imperfect especially for rare species and small populations. If populations are unequally detectable across groups to be compared, results are biased and do not reflect reality (Kery 2004). Such unequal detectability despite the use of standardised methods can for instance be caused by environmental or climatic variables. Statistical methods for estimating site occupancy are useful tools for analysing the significance of monitoring data (MacKenzie et al. 2002) and have been successfully applied for monitoring amphibian distribution in terrestrial (Bailey et al. 2004) and aquatic (Schmidt 2005) habitats. Crested newts might be missed during surveys especially when submerged vegetation is dense and deep water zones are extended (e.g. Beebee 1990). However, Cooke (1995) showed that survey results at a secure site using night counting procedures were positively related to numbers gained by bottle traps. In our study the detection probabilities for both adults and larvae were high compared to a related study dealing with three anuran species (Schmidt 2005). We did not test climatic effects on our detection histories but personal experience shows that especially bottle traps are effective independent of weather conditions. We achieved the highest detection probability for adult newts in the second survey, probably caused by the combination of night counting and bottle traps. The increasing probability in detection of larvae is most probably explained by the survey dates. Altogether the use of combined methods can in our case be regarded as adequate and successful. Habitat features of studied ponds Many studies in core distribution areas have dealt with the question what might make a good Crested newt pond (e.g. Swan & Oldham 1994, Oldham et al. 2000). According to Blab & Blab (1981) shading, pond area and density of submerged vegetation are the three relevant pond characteristics for the abundance of Crested newts. In a study from Western France shading represented a key feature for the abundance of larval Triturus newts, suggesting that the successional stage of the pond is important (Sztatecsny et al. 2004). Our results reflect these findings to a certain degree. Shading and density of submerged vegetation had significant effects on pond occupancy in our study, while pond area was of no importance for Crested newt presence. Cooke et al. (1994) regarded ponds with less than 10 % shade as ideal for populations in Great Britain. In a study from the German province of Lower Saxony Crested newts are missing from ponds with a degree of shading higher than 40 % (Filoda 1981). Although in the province of Salzburg the number of ponds located in open areas is low due to intensive land use, and most of the surveyed ponds are to some extent associated with forests or shrubberies, the majority of occupied ponds showed a degree of shading below 50 %. Positive effects of submerged vegetation density were reported by Oldham (1994) who suggested a total macrophyte cover of 70-80 % as ideal for Crested newt ponds. While in our study this effect was high but not significant for adults, we found a highly significant effect for the presence of larvae. Atkins (1998) reported 500-750 m² as typical pond size for Triturus cristatus in Great Britain. A minimal pond size of 50 m² and a minimal pond depth of 50 cm are given as key figures for the whole superspecies, with T. carnifex being the species with the highest ecological amplitude (Arntzen 2003). In areas with high densities of Crested newt populations, pond size and depth play an important role, because there are simply more ponds to choose from. For Crested newt larvae there is some evidence that intermediate pond sizes may be favourable (Van Buskirk 2005). In Salzburg these features have no significant effects on their presence. Perhaps here the low number of ponds forces them to take what they can find. The manipulation of ponds by means of fish introduction is one of the major causes for population declines throughout many parts of the distribution range of Crested newts (Thiesmeier & Kupfer 2000). This habitat variable showed no significantly negative effect in our study. Possible explanations might be that on the one hand introduction of fish into most of our studied ponds happened very recently and the number of fish is very low in some cases. Species richness In the province of Salzburg ponds occupied by Crested newts in most instances represent aquatic habitats of high value for amphibians in general. We observed significant differences in amphibian species richness between occupied and unoccupied ponds. Especially the Smooth newt (Lissotriton vulgaris) and the Tree frog (Hyla arborea), both listed as endangered in the current Red List (Kyek & Maletzky 2006), obviously need similar habitat features in our region. This fact can also be observed vice versa, as a practical conservation project in the years 2002 and 2003 showed. Two of our surveyed ponds (Freimoos 2 and Freimoos 3, see Tab. 1) were created especially for the needs of Tree frogs during a translocation project and were colonised by Crested newts one year after the ponds were created (Kyek et al. in press). Conclusions and implications for future programmes Crested newts (Triturus cristatus superspecies) are at the uppermost level of legal protection in Austria, underlying European (EU habitats directive), national (national Red List) and regional (species protection decree, nature conservation law) regulations. As they are listed in Annex II and IV of the EU habitats directive, the establishment of special protected areas (Natura 2000) as well as monitoring programmes and enhancement measures for aquatic and terrestrial habitats are demanded. Nevertheless a comparably strong decline of population numbers could be observed for no other amphibian species during recent decades and no protected areas have been declared for the needs of these species. At the end of 2005 no occupied Crested newt pond is documented within the range of Natura 2000 areas in Salzburg (Kyek & Maletzky 2006). The effective conservation status of the Crested newt species (Triturus cristatus, T. carnifex) in this area is critical and the high degree of legal protection does not appear to be reflected in conservation benefit. Even intact and frequently reproducing populations show unfavourable conservation status in terms of population sizes, quality of the terrestrial habitat and degree of isolation (Maletzky unpublished data). We strongly call for the initiation of measures to avoid a further decline of these species, not least due to their high significance as indicators of amphibian richness and their great value for science, being located in an area where two species are occurring narrowly sympatric and hybrid populations exist (e.g. Freytag, 1978, Arntzen 2003, Maletzky unpublished data). Crested newts in this area largely depend on artificial ponds. The focus of future conservation efforts must lie in the creation of pond networks, including new artificial ponds as well as the enhancement of old ponds and the parallel development of migration corridors. For aiding as many species as possible, a number of connected smaller ponds may be preferable compared with single large ones (Oertli et al. 2002). Furthermore new ponds should be placed in reachable distances to existing populations and as isolated as possible from human infrastructure preventing the introduction of allochthonous fish and rubbish (Williams et al. 1999). Natural variability of carbon dioxide and net epilimnetic production in the surface waters of boreal lakes of different sizes Carol A. Kelly¹ University of Manitoba, Department of Microbiology, Winnipeg, Manitoba R3T 2N2, Canada Everett Fee,² Patricia S. Ramlal,³ John W. M. Rudd, Raymond H. Hesslein, Cory Anema, and Eva U. Schindler Freshwater Institute, Department of Fisheries and Oceans, 501 University Crescent, Winnipeg, Manitoba R3T 2N6, Canada Abstract The variability of surface water carbon dioxide concentration, or partial pressure (\( pCO_2 \)), was studied in 11 lakes of greatly varying size (2.4 ha up to 8 million ha) in Northwest Ontario, Canada. Six of these lakes were chosen to be as similar as possible in all respects except surface area (the Northwest Ontario Lake Size Series [NOLSS], which range from 88 to 35,000 ha). Spatial and temporal variability of \( pCO_2 \) within a single lake was no greater in the larger lakes than in the smaller lakes. Interannual variability was significant and synchronous, which indicates that weather patterns were important and affected the different lakes within the region in a similar manner. However, annual \( pCO_2 \) averages were not related to annual differences in planktonic photosynthetic activity, measured by \( ^{14}CO_2 \) fixation. In the six NOLSS lakes, there was not a significant relationship of average \( pCO_2 \) with lake size. For all 11 lakes, however, there was a significant negative correlation of \( pCO_2 \) with lake size, which was likely due to several characteristics of the very small and very large lakes that covaried with size. The larger lakes were deeper and had longer water residence times and lower DOC, which suggests lower CO\(_2\) production from allochthonous organic carbon inputs. Also, the ratio of epilimnetic sediment area/epilimnetic volume (\( A_e/V_e \)) was smaller in the larger lakes, which likely resulted in lower rates of recycling of fixed carbon to CO\(_2\) during summer stratification. Measurement of dissolved CO\(_2\) in the surface waters of lakes is as useful as measurement of dissolved oxygen in determining net biological activity in lakes, especially when examining interactions between lakes and their watersheds (Kling et al. 1991; Dillon and Molot 1997). For example, the finding that average CO\(_2\) concentrations in many lakes are above atmospheric equilibrium indicates that allochthonous contributions to lake metabolism often exceed net autochthonous fixation (Cole et al. 1994). This link with watersheds is demonstrated, in a series of Wisconsin lakes, by the positive correlation of surface water CO\(_2\) with the ratio of drainage area to lake area, and with the extent of wetland area surrounding the lake (Hope et al. 1996). Artificial lakes (reservoirs) tend to have higher CO\(_2\) concentrations than natural lakes due to decomposition of flooded vegetation or peat, which could also be considered “allochthonous” carbon sources (Duchemin et al. 1995; Kelly et al. 1997). Where degradation of allochthonous carbon is small, or quantifiable, measurements of CO\(_2\) can give information about the extent of use of autochthonous carbon, i.e., the fraction of photosynthetically fixed CO\(_2\) that is respired after fixation by the algae, grazers, and the rest of the lake’s biota. In addition to biological processes within lakes that affect CO\(_2\), external inputs via streams or groundwater inflows contribute dissolved CO\(_2\) (Kratz et al. 1997) and bicarbonate ions (HCO\(_3^-\)) that can be converted to CO\(_2\) after entering lakes (Dillon and Molot 1997). It is difficult to distinguish between inorganic and organic allochthonous sources of CO\(_2\), but the combination of dissolved oxygen measurement with CO\(_2\) measurements is a promising approach because organic degradation consumes oxygen, whereas inorganic inputs should have no effect on oxygen (Carignan 1998). Previous studies have examined the diel (Sellers et al. 1995) or seasonal variability of CO\(_2\) concentrations in surface waters (Hesslein et al. 1990; Cole et al. 1994) of one or a few lakes. Geographic variability has also been studied, with the data set including a wide variety of lakes, but with few data points from each lake (Cole et al. 1994). The study reported here is the first to carry out long-term (8 yr), regular interval measurements on a fairly large set of lakes in one geographic location and to include measurements of photosynthesis and other parameters that can be used to understand patterns in CO\(_2\). These lakes are generally remote, with minimal anthropogenic impacts. At the core of the study were six remote boreal lakes, the northwest Ontario lake size series (NOLSS, Fee and Hecky 1992). These lakes were chosen to be similar in most characteristics except for surface area, which ranged from 88 to 35,000 ha. We also studied five additional Ontario lakes, extending the size range down to 2.4 ha and up to over 8 million ha.
